Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.
On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.
The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."
Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.
"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."
Ragheb argued that the United States' in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

Turkey advances mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan amid Houthi attacks
Turkey took a step toward expanding its security presence in the Gulf on Tuesday by submitting the trilateral Mecca Joint Defense Agreement to parliament for ratification, Reuters reported.
The treaty, signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, moves NATO’s second-largest army closer to a formal defense commitment to Riyadh as Saudi Arabia faces attacks by the Houthis.
Under the pact's primary clause, an armed attack on any member state is treated as an attack on all, requiring signatories to use all necessary means to eliminate threats to each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity, according to text seen by Reuters.

Iran shifts attacks to ships' engine rooms, inflicting damage in Persian Gulf: report
Iran's IRGC is increasingly targeting ships' engine rooms in the Persian Gulf, inflicting damage that can cripple vessels for months and trigger expensive repairs, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.
Shipping and maritime security officials reported a rise in engine-room damage, with strikes sparking fires, disabling power and propulsion systems, and leaving vessels out of service amid costly repairs.
“What we’re seeing is an increase in the frequency of attacks, and therefore, more damage in engine rooms and disabling fire,” Phillip Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, told the outlet.
“Attacks often focus on the engine room or the bridge of the ships as it maximizes damage while keeping the risk of an oil spill relatively low,” Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at BIMCO, said.
He also warned that “there are significant risks of crew injuries when these areas of the ship are hit.”

“We destroyed the platform that launched the ballistic missile that was fired at Riyadh today,” coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki confirmed on X.
The coalition also shared footage showing the tracking and targeting process.

Speaking in Tehran with visiting Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pezeshkian blamed the United States for the ongoing conflict.
“All regional problems, from escalating tensions to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, stem from US warmongering,” Pezeshkian said, according to Iran's state-run broadcaster, IRIB.
“The Americans must explain why they started the war and embroiled themselves and the world in it.”
He added: “Before any negotiations, they must first end the pressure and threats and lift sanctions,” the president added.
Iran-linked terror probe at RAF Fairford intensifies as 2 re-arrested
British counterterrorism police re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence and involvement in the suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford in September.
The arrests, made under the National Security Act, involve a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, both from the London borough of Westminster.
"Our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said Tuesday.
He added that specialist teams are pursuing multiple lines of inquiry in what he described as a "hugely complex investigation."
The air base in Gloucestershire had been used by U.S. bombers to carry out strikes against Iran before the initial security breach when five men were arrested outside the facility.
U.S. B-1 bombers were withdrawn from the base after the arrests.
A total of seven suspects were initially arrested and released on bail, including the 24-year-old arrested near the base and the 25-year-old later arrested in London.
Hegseth confirms Israel visit, private Netanyahu meeting

"I was there visiting our troops," Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisconsin.
"Had a chance to talk to the Prime Minister. Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about, but they've been good partners and I appreciate that."
Hegseth’s remarks follow reports that the high-level meeting took place at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel.
According to sources, the private talks centered heavily on regional security concerns, including threats posed by Iran.
Hegseth also met with U.S. service members stationed in the region under U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM).
Fox News' Liz Friden contributed to this report.
Iran blasts US arrest warrant for Cuba's Raul Castro as illegal
Tehran rejected a U.S. arrest warrant targeting former Cuban President Raul Castro on Tuesday, labeling the move an illegal and criminal act of foreign intervention.
In an official statement, the Iranian Foreign Ministry also denounced U.S. economic sanctions and intimidation tactics against Cuban officials, framing Washington's pressure campaign as a violation of the U.N. Charter and international law.
The statement followed an arrest warrant filed by Florida prosecutors charging Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.

articles.title: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans - Vox
articles.summary: How the Iran war is ruining Saudi Arabia’s plans  VoxEverything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman  The EconomistSaudi Arabia’s Military Limitations Are Being Exposed by Houthi Attacks  WSJWhy the Houthis Are So Hard to Defeat  Bloomberg.comHow Saudi Arabia Created the Yemen It Fears  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
As the US-Iran war drags on, the damage is being felt regionally: Saudi Arabia experienced the worst attack in over a decade earlier this month, when Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia struck an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. The strike killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Saudi Arabia responded with missile attacks on Yemen, striking oil facilities, and the Houthis have launched more strikes of their own, targeting Saudi oil infrastructure.
The dueling strikes are the latest development in a decade-plus of conflict between Saudi and the Houthis, a political and military group that controls part of northern Yemen, which had been on pause until earlier this year after a 2022 ceasefire. But the Iran war, and Houthi affiliation with Iran’s network of proxy groups, mean the current violence has far-reaching implications for the US, Israel, and the global energy economy.
It also threatens more than just Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil industry: As Gregg Carlstrom, a Middle East correspondent for The Economist, explains, the attacks cut at the heart of the country’s project to evolve into a destination for foreign investment, travel, tourism, and more. On Monday, the country’s upcoming Future Investment Initiative was postponed until 2027.
Carlstrom, who is based in Riyadh, spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram how the attack has been received inside Saudi Arabia, why it comes at an especially bad time for the country, and how President Donald Trump might — or might not — get more involved.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Can you help us understand how the Houthis have such a presence in the country right now? Are they infiltrating the country? Are they already there?
They’re shooting from outside the country. They’re shooting from Yemen. The Houthis are a group that’s been around for a few decades. They were originally a local insurgency in Yemen that was fighting against the Yemeni government. They originate from the northern part of Yemen, but they were able to gain control of large parts of that country from 2014 onwards. Ali Abdullah Saleh, the longtime dictator of Yemen, was overthrown during the Arab Spring and the Houthis were able to seize a large chunk of territory.
They are effectively in control of most of the population centers in Yemen. They have received increasing support from Iran, which has provided them with weapons, with money, with know-how, and technical expertise. And they have used that to build an arsenal of drones and missiles, which they are using now to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia.
And was there a particular reason they targeted the airport in Riyadh? Were they trying to send a message here?
If you listen to the messaging from the Houthis, they are trying to describe this as almost a like-for-like campaign, where you’ve had years in which the Saudi-led coalition, which invaded Yemen in 2015, has been imposing a blockade of Yemeni airspace, has been restricting flights in and out of that country.
And so the Houthis describe this publicly as being a retaliation in kind, but I think they’ve also just figured out that attacks on airports are a very effective way to cause economic disruption in Saudi Arabia. You prevent not just people from flying in and out but also, as we’ve seen disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, a lot of cargo that these countries depend on for daily needs are coming in by air instead.
Carrying out these sorts of attacks, shutting down the airport in a capital city, is a very effective way for the Houthis to impose economic pain on the Saudis.
And I guess on some level it makes the country feel insecure. How is that making Saudi Arabia’s leader feel right now? What’s his response been?
It comes at a very difficult time for the Saudi leadership because they are supposed to be hosting a number of events this month where Saudi will be playing a role on the world stage.
There’s something called the World Petroleum Congress that is taking place this week [October 11–15], which is normally a big event that draws executives from top oil and gas companies. Many of them canceled their participation because of the attacks on the airport.
Then they are supposed to be hosting the [now-postponed] Future Investment Initiative, which is something often known outside Saudi Arabia as “Davos in the Desert.” It’s the sort of flagship investment conference that takes place here every year. It draws a who’s who of global finance.
For a country that is trying to diversify its economy, a country that is trying to attract foreign investment and make itself into a hub for finance and travel and tourism, these sorts of attacks are very detrimental to those goals.
And this is coming as Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the rest of the leadership in the country is really trying to establish Saudi Arabia as the premier economic hub in the region. The stakes are really high for him right now?
They are. And just about everything that they are trying to do is being disrupted by what’s happened over the past few weeks.
If you look at travel, for example, the Public Investment Fund, which is the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, last year launched a new airline, Riyadh Air, which they are hoping will eventually compete with Emirates or Qatar Airways, the really big carriers in the Gulf.
That airline was just getting into regular operations this summer where they were growing their fleet, they were growing their network of destinations. And then suddenly this happens and their home base in Riyadh is shut down. They have moved some of their planes out of Riyadh to other airports to keep them safe from Houthi attacks. Obviously, it’s very disruptive for trying to build an air carrier.
In Riyadh itself, the financial district — this sort of long-planned attempt to set up a banking hub that might rival the one in Dubai — had just started to get going over the past couple of years, when you had banks and other financial services firms moving in there. Everybody who works there has now been told to work remotely for the foreseeable future because there is a concern about possible Houthi attacks against skyscrapers and the financial district.
Everything they are trying to do, from finance to travel to trade, all of it is being disrupted and threatened by what’s happening in Yemen.
What options does he have to reassure investors and the world really that he can protect the country and maybe especially his airport, where a bunch of the investment is focused?
The airport, I think, is going to be difficult to reassure people about. You can install additional air defenses there. You can move more batteries and more interceptors there, but at the end of the day, no air defense system is hermetic. There’s no 100 percent guarantee that you’re going to shoot down every incoming projectile.
As long as there is this ongoing war between the Houthis and Yemen and the Saudis, I think people might have ongoing concerns about the airport. You have to resolve that underlying issue to give people confidence.
Now, how do you try to resolve that? If you’re Saudi Arabia right now, you have two bad options. One is you keep fighting. You try to militarily defeat the Houthis or at least force them to accept a renewed ceasefire.
The other option is you cut a deal. You try to offer the Houthis some concessions that might encourage them to go back to the ceasefire. That’s going to be very costly for Saudi Arabia. I’ve heard that the Houthis are demanding probably billions of dollars of financial concessions where they would want the Saudis to offer some money for reconstruction and to pay the salaries of Yemeni civil servants working in Houthi-controlled areas.
If you are the Saudi leadership right now, neither one is really a good option.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a pretty strong relationship with the president of the United States, who’s very sympathetic to Saudi Arabia and Saudi investment. Has he appealed to President Trump for help here yet?
He has. He’s done so repeatedly over the past month or so, asking not just for support with the Saudi campaign in Yemen, but for America to carry out its own airstrikes in Yemen. And the response so far from Donald Trump has been to refuse that.
For the US to get involved in a bigger way, there are some practical constraints at the moment where a lot of American military assets are tied up in the Strait of Hormuz trying to keep that open, keep oil flowing through the Strait. And so the response from Trump has been disappointing for the Saudi Crown prince. The US is providing intelligence support. It’s helping on that front, but it is not directly getting involved in the war in Yemen.

articles.title: How the Houthis Threaten Saudi Oil - The National Interest
articles.summary: How the Houthis Threaten Saudi Oil  The National Interest
articles.full_text:
Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure could keep oil above $100 a barrel and pull Pakistan, Turkey, and others into a widening web of regional conflicts.
While the outcome of the Iran war is of considerable geoeconomic importance, Yemen’s Houthis have the potential to be an equally daunting threat to the global economy, especially with an eye to energy prices and entangling alliances.
The Houthis occupy an important strategic location, neighboring Saudi Arabia and sitting across from the politically tense Horn of Africa. In 2025, they amply demonstrated an ability to hit Red Sea shipping, which resulted in US air attacks, a situation that later that year morphed into a US-Houthi truce. Since July 2026, they have driven south into the parts of Yemen they do not control, seeking to gain greater control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait while launching ongoing drone and missile attacks against Saudi infrastructure.
Why Iran and China Have Armed the Houthis
The Houthis’ rise has been aided for over a decade by Iran, which has found it strategically useful to help a fellow Shia community, surrounded by Sunnis (most of Yemen’s population and neighboring Saudi Arabia and Oman). Tehran has supplied them with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and anti-ship weapons. At war off and on with the rest of Yemen since 2004, the formerly marginalized Houthis are now one of the region’s most effective military forces. China has also helped the Houthis, selling them Chinese-made components for missiles in exchange for immunity for Chinese-flagged ships in the Red Sea.
While Iran may see the Houthis as a junior partner, they don’t. As former US ambassador Barbara Leaf, who served as the US assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in the Biden administration, noted, “They do not see themselves as the junior partner to Iran or least of all a proxy. They regard themselves as a power unto themselves. They’re determined to demonstrate that.”
The Houthis have a sense of grievance vis-à-vis the Saudis, whom they regard as unworthy of guardianship of Mecca due to their ties to the United States and, by extension, Israel. Moreover, the Saudis have meddled in Yemeni affairs for decades. It is time for payback.
How Houthi Attacks on Saudi Oil Threaten Global Prices
In early October, they attacked Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure and Riyadh’s international airport, killing 18 people and injuring others. In a sense, the Houthis are bringing the fight to Saudi Arabia where it hurts most—its energy sector and sectors that are central to the government’s efforts to diversify away from oil. Bringing that point home, the Houthis attacked the headquarters of their neighbor’s national oil company, Saudi Aramco, causing extensive damage in what is regarded as the nerve center of Aramco’s operations.
The Houthis are threatening to continue to strike airports and energy infrastructure in the Saudi interior and urging global shipping companies, citizens, and employees at these locations to evacuate. Moreover, they regard those foreign companies as “legitimate targets.”
Why do we care? Global oil prices are already tracking over $100 a barrel. If the Houthis can destroy enough of the Saudi energy sector by hitting refineries, knocking out pipelines, and threatening shipping in the Red Sea, they can keep pressure on global oil prices, which helps their ally, Iran, which needs ongoing economic pressure on the US.
How the Houthis Are Testing Saudi Arabia’s New Defense Pact
But the situation is even more complicated. The United States, which has a considerable military buildup in the region and is expected to take more aggressive action against Iran after the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, has been notable for keeping Yemen’s chaotic and Byzantine civil wars at arm’s length. In turn, the US conflict with Iran and the related damage to Saudi infrastructure has forced Riyadh to acknowledge that Washington cannot be counted on to fully defend its national security. This was a motivating dynamic for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. Signed in August 2026, the agreement stipulates that “any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as any attack against them all.” If this was intended to scare the Houthis into stopping their attacks on Saudi Arabia, it failed.
The Houthis pose a geopolitical dilemma to Pakistan and Turkey. The kingdom is a major source of oil for both countries and Riyadh has been a very important financial supporter of the heavily indebted Pakistani state. Pakistan has borrowed $3 billion from the Saudis, which was recently provided to help stabilize the South Asian country’s economy. Considering this, it is no surprise that Pakistan has committed to the deployment of a military force to Saudi Arabia, with Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif stating that his commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty is “unwavering.”
Why Pakistan and Turkey Are Wary of Fighting the Houthis
But Pakistan’s position is more complicated. It shares a lengthy and porous border with Iran, has sought to be an honest broker in negotiations between Tehran and Washington, and is attempting to improve relations with the United States after having built up a significant dependence on China (which proved difficult in dealing with Pakistan’s debt restructuring). Additionally, Pakistan’s relations with Afghanistan’s Taliban government are tense, with border conflicts as well as Pakistani aircraft strikes inside Afghanistan. Pakistan wants the Taliban government to stop militants (mainly from the Pakistani Taliban) from using Afghan territory to launch attacks inside Pakistan.
Although Turkey has sent support staff and drones to Saudi Arabia, it also appears to be reluctant to directly engage the Houthis. Despite the US economic embargo on Iran, Turkey has a large trading relationship with its neighbor, with a hoped-for target of $30 billion in cross-border trade. Moreover, Turkey is playing a significant role in Syria, a country in which Iran believes it has a special interest, especially as it serves as a conduit of weapons and funds to Lebanon’s Hezbollah. One last item in this situation is that Turkey is a NATO member. Would its engagement in a war with the Houthis involve NATO?
How Overlapping Conflicts Stretch from the Caspian to the Horn of Africa
The Houthi threat is layered onto an arc of potentially overlapping conflicts and strategic alliances that stretches from the Caspian Sea to the Horn of Africa. The Iran war has engaged the United States, Israel, the Gulf states, Egypt, and Jordan. The Houthis are engaging Saudi Arabia, and Turkey and Pakistan are now being drawn into the conflict. Ukrainian forces have attacked Russian assets in the Caspian Sea while Israel bombed Iranian assets on the same body of water. Across the Red Sea, fighting has returned to Ethiopia vis-à-vis the Tigray (internally) and Eritrea. Russia has gained a naval base at Port Sudan and its mercenaries are reportedly in action in Sudan’s nasty civil war; Turkey is providing military advisors to Somalia’s central government; and Israel is the first country to officially recognize Somaliland, home to one of the region’s best ports, Berbera (which used to be a naval base for the Soviet Union during the Cold War).
The United Arab Emirates has been an active supporter of Ethiopia, providing it with investment and military assistance, and its Dubai World is upgrading the port at Berbera. The Persian Gulf country has also been active in Ethiopia, home of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) at the headwaters of the Blue Nile. That support puts it at odds with Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia, and Sudan, which in early October held a summit stressing their concern over the GERD and its impact on Nile water flow and territorial sovereignty across the Horn of Africa.
Rounding out the picture, China is a major economic power throughout the region, as the largest trading partner of Iran, Iraq, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, and Pakistan. For its part, in 2025 China imported a little over 50 percent of its oil from the Middle East, making it an interested party. It also has naval forces based in Djibouti, along with the United States, France, Japan, Italy, and South Korea. China prefers to be a behind-the-scenes actor, but the longer the conflict in the Persian Gulf extends, the deeper the energy bite. The situation also increases the scrutiny of China’s role with the Houthis as well as its ongoing trade relations with Iran.
Why the Houthis Pose a Dilemma for Washington
Into this cauldron of Byzantine geopolitics, a broader conflict with the Houthis will intensify already high regional tensions. It also offers up a scenario in which various regional powers become more active and are drawn into local conflicts as in the Pakistani and Turkish cases.
The Houthis pose a major problem for the United States—it is already fighting one war; it does not need another. Indeed, while the Trump administration condemns the Houthi advance down the Yemeni coastline, the United States has held off any military responses. It has also been reported that the Houthis have reassured the United States that the 2025 ceasefire between them is still in force, meaning that only Saudi shipping will be attacked, not US shipping. This puts the Houthi problem on hold for now, but ongoing damage to Saudi oil infrastructure keeps a foot on the gas pedal, something that is obviously a concern for President Donald Trump.
For now, the Houthis have a strong geoeconomic card to play if they can radically reduce the Saudi ability to supply global oil and gas markets as well as complicate the passage of commerce in the Red Sea. The even larger risk is that the arc from the Caspian Sea to the Nile has too many entangling alliances, involving regional and global powers. As with the Balkans in 1914, at some point there is a real danger that the fuse is lit.

"We are committed to completing the elimination of the Iranian regime," Netanyahu said in a statement released by his office. "I have discussed this with Trump many times, including the day before yesterday."
Meanwhile, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also discussed Iran with Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran.
Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the prime minister, later confirmed to Reuters that Netanyahu had met with Hegseth at the Uvda air force base in Israel's southern Negev desert region.
Netanyahu and Hegseth discussed "the threats in the region" and the U.S.-Israel partnership in dealing both offensively and defensively with those threats, he said in a brief phone call.
Hegseth also thanked Israel for hosting U.S. forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump's support for the prime minister.
"There's a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion," Spielman said.
On Sunday, Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel, the country's first ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.
The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Hegseth's visit.
Hegseth earlier posted on X that he had visited U.S. service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.
He did not specify where he had met with the forces.
Hegseth's visit comes as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
U.S. and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he's not seeking to attack Iran before the Oct. 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before U.S. midterm elections in November.
Israel has hosted additional U.S. forces, including military aircraft, since at least February as part of the war with Iran.

Saudi forces said they intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh Tuesday, following a danger warning and reports of explosions in the capital.
Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led military coalition backing Yemen's government, confirmed the kingdom intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi militia targeting Riyadh.
Two blasts shook Riyadh, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalists in the capital.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh to alert for a potential danger," the Saudi civil defense said in a statement on X, formerly Twitter. But minutes later, the civil defense lifted the alert, saying "the danger has passed."
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have escalated, forcing the postponement of a major investment conference and undermining Riyadh's hopes of attracting greater foreign capital and diversifying its economy. The deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis have forced Riyadh's airport to close.
The Saudi air force regularly targets the Houthis in retaliation amid fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and the Riyadh-backed government. In July, a fragile 2022 truce collapsed after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Sanaa, Yemen's capital, in defiance of Riyadh's control over Yemeni airspace, triggering a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began striking its ships, territory and oil facilities, before uprooting Yemeni government forces from Red Sea coastline positions in a swift campaign in September.
Earlier Monday, the Yemeni army said clashes and airstrikes killed 129 Houthi fighters and wounded 176 others over the past two days in the southwestern province of Taiz.
In a statement, the army's Taiz Military Axis Command said government forces continued their offensive against Houthi positions in the al-Misrakh district, south of Taiz city, for a second consecutive day.
Local fighters and residents supported the operation, which inflicted heavy losses on the Houthis, the command added.
It said army units also raided a Houthi position in the al-Aqrud front, killing and wounding several fighters. It added warplanes conducted 13 airstrikes Monday night, targeting Houthi positions, weapons, military equipment, ammunition depots and gatherings across Taiz province.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the army's claims.
Taiz holds strategic importance because it connects Yemen's northern and southern provinces and serves as a vital transportation and supply corridor between the interim capital Aden and the country's central and northern regions. The province also includes the Red Sea port of Mokha, near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb strait.
Since fighting intensified in July, government forces and their allies have announced advances on several fronts, including regaining control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait and areas of the Dhubab district.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their siege of Taiz city from surrounding northern, western and eastern highlands following advances in parts of the province's countryside.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa, the capital, and several other provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country's southern and eastern provinces.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia should join US-led push for change in Iran, analyst says - Iran International
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia should join US-led push for change in Iran, analyst says  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia should join forces with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates to help bring about political change in Iran, rather than continue policies that have failed to contain Tehran's regional influence, an analyst told Iran International.
The Islamic Republic's support for Yemen's Houthis has exposed the limits of Saudi military power and diplomacy, making a broader coalition against Iran necessary, said Hussain Abdul-Hussain, a research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“I'm not saying the Marines should land anywhere in Tehran,” Abdul-Hussain said. “I'm just saying push the regime enough so that the other Iranians can take over.”
The proposed strategy, he said, would draw on the US-led coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991, with Saudi Arabia providing regional political support for a campaign aimed at weakening the Islamic Republic and enabling Iranians to determine their country's political future.
Such a coalition could fundamentally alter the regional balance of power and influence the calculations of China and Russia, Abdul-Hussain added.
Iran's Houthi leverage
The Houthis have emerged as one of the Islamic Republic's most effective regional allies, maintaining their military capabilities despite years of Saudi-led operations and pressure on other Iran-backed armed groups.
Their geographical distance from Israel has also made them more difficult to weaken than Hezbollah in Lebanon or Iran-aligned militias in Iraq, according to Abdul-Hussain.
The challenge, he said, has become more pronounced since the withdrawal of Emirati forces from Yemen following divisions within the Saudi-led coalition.
Pro-UAE militias had provided some of the coalition's most effective ground forces, leaving Saudi Arabia increasingly dependent on air power and Yemeni government forces weakened by corruption, inflated troop numbers and divisions, Abdul-Hussain said.
Airstrikes alone cannot defeat an armed group operating from mountainous terrain and fortified positions, he argued, drawing comparisons with Israel's experience fighting Hezbollah in 2006 and 2023.
The absence of reliable ground partners has therefore allowed the Houthis to remain a persistent military challenge despite Saudi Arabia's superior conventional capabilities.
The group's operations also serve Iran's wider regional strategy by placing Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping routes within reach of an Iranian ally.
Recent Houthi advances and strikes on Saudi territory reflect a broader Iranian message that disruptions to its own oil exports could be accompanied by pressure on other regional producers, particularly as Saudi Arabia shifts exports toward the Bab el-Mandeb shipping route, Abdul-Hussain added.
Saudi diplomatic failures
Saudi Arabia's continued diplomatic engagement with the Islamic Republic has failed to reduce the security challenge posed by Iran's regional allies, Abdul-Hussain said.
Maintaining an ambassador in Tehran and inviting Revolutionary Guards officials to Saudi National Day celebrations, even as Saudi energy infrastructure faces missile strikes, sends a message of weakness rather than diplomatic pragmatism, he argued.
The UAE, despite its smaller size and closer geographical proximity to Iran, had previously demonstrated greater willingness to sever diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic, according to Abdul-Hussain.
Saudi Arabia's diplomatic outreach to Turkey and Pakistan has also produced limited practical support against the Houthis and the Revolutionary Guards, he said.
Abdul-Hussain attributed part of the problem to a Saudi leadership structure in which advisers are reluctant to challenge prevailing assumptions, leaving decision-makers without a credible alternative to their existing strategy.
“They have to swallow their pride with the Emiratis and the Israelis,” Abdul-Hussain said. “This is the key.”
Restoring cooperation with Abu Dhabi and establishing open relations with Israel would provide the foundation for a more effective regional alignment against Iran, he added.
Such cooperation would need to be public rather than confined to private security arrangements, particularly because Israeli participation could expose Israeli shipping to additional Houthi operations.
Saudi Arabia's decision to condition normalization with Israel on Palestinian statehood has further complicated the formation of an anti-Iran coalition, Abdul-Hussain said.
The shift, he noted, has moved Riyadh away from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's earlier emphasis on prioritizing Saudi national interests, without producing corresponding security benefits for the kingdom.
Coalition against Iran
A coalition modeled on the international military campaign that expelled Saddam Hussein's forces from Kuwait in 1991 could provide a framework for confronting the Islamic Republic without a US ground invasion of Iran, Abdul-Hussain said.
Saudi Arabia played a central role in assembling regional support for that campaign, lending political legitimacy to a military operation led by the United States.
A similar alignment involving Washington, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Israel could apply sustained pressure on Iran's ruling establishment while leaving the ultimate outcome to Iranians themselves, according to the analyst.
“Throw all the chips behind President Trump and the war on Iran, and push for regime change,” Abdul-Hussain said.
The proposed approach would mark a departure from Saudi Arabia's efforts to balance diplomatic relations with Iran against military operations targeting its regional allies.
Rather than continuing to absorb the costs of confronting the Houthis without weakening their principal backer, Saudi Arabia should help organize a broader campaign directed at the Islamic Republic itself, Abdul-Hussain argued.
The central objective, in his view, would not be a foreign occupation of Iran but sufficient external pressure to create an opportunity for Iranians to replace the country's ruling establishment.

articles.full_text:
Washington Report on Middle East Affairs, November/December 2026, pp. 60-61
Special Report
By Dr. P. Bruce McLaren
OPERATION “DAWN OF YEMEN” was launched on Oct. 5, 2026, by Saudi-backed forces to retake the strategic Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea, from Ansar Allah (commonly referred to as the Houthis). As we went to press the United States was resisting requests from the Saudis to take part in a combat role. Why?
In 1939, Winston Churchill famously characterized Russia as “A riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma.” He also offered the solution to the conundrum: “Perhaps there is a key. That key is Russian national interest.
The same observation may be applied to the Houthis.
Conventionally, the Houthis have been characterized as regional proxies of Iran. Recent developments suggest this perspective understates their autonomy. The group increasingly operates as an independent actor, playing Washington and Riyadh against one another. On the geopolitical chessboard of the Middle East, it is increasingly clear that the Houthis are no pawns.
The airstrikes launched by Israel and the United States on Feb. 28, 2026, marked a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict with Iran. Rather than representing a new fracture, this action served as a severe acceleration of a decades-long conflict into open hostility.
In the current dispute between the United States and Iran, the primary conflict is not being played out in a conventional war. Instead, the real fight involves the strategic control of global trade. The key tactical target has been the Strait of Hormuz, which governs the flow of oil exiting the Persian Gulf.
The theater of operations has since expanded across the broader Middle East, drawing in regional aligned groups such as the Houthis on the Arabian Peninsula. Consequently, the Bab al-Mandab has emerged as a second critical maritime chokepoint. Because this strait acts as the primary commercial artery for physical goods between Asian and European ports, the dual disruption of both the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz carries profound, far-reaching economic implications for global markets.
The primary power behind the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz is Iran. Providing a political and ideological summary of modern Iran is relatively straightforward. Iran is committed to charting its own course and resisting foreign coercion. Since 1979 Iran has been a fundamentalist Islamic theocratic republic that has adopted Twelver Shi’a Islam as its official religion, an ideological framework that persists today.
The principal actors behind the blockade of the Bab al-Mandab are the Houthis. An analysis of the identity and beliefs of the Houthis presents a more complex challenge. The Houthis are best understood as a political and military organization rooted in the al-Houthi family, a prominent clan from the mountainous northern region of Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula. While the Houthis share Shi’a alignment with Iran, they adhere to Fiver Shi’a Islam (Zaydi Islam) rather than Twelver Shi’a Islam.
As the majority Shi’a sect, Twelvers recognize 12 divinely appointed Imams descended from the Prophet’s lineage, beginning with his son-in-law, Ali. They believe the 12th Imam, the Mahdi, entered a state of occultation in 874 CE and will return before the Day of Judgment.
A distinct minority sect within the Shi’a branch are The Fivers, a term derived from a dispute as to the rightful succession of the fifth Shi’a Imam. Fivers argue that the true fifth Imam was Zayd Ibn Ali (695–740 CE). Consequently, Fivers are referred to as Zaydis.
The majority of the world’s Zaydi population resides in Yemen. The earliest Zaydi dynasty in Yemen was founded in 897 CE by al-Hadi ila al-Haqq Yahya, a direct descendant of Muhammad, who established the Zaydi Imamate of Yemen.
Over the subsequent millennium, 60 of the region’s 73 Zaydi Imams traced their direct lineage back to Yahya. The region’s final Imam, Muhammad al-Badr, fled the country following a coup in 1962 and later died in exile in London in 1996. The Zaydi Imamate in Yemen has remained vacant since his departure.
The Zaydi school of thought occupies a unique position within the broader Islamic framework, balancing elements of both Sunni and Shi’a traditions. Zaydi jurisprudence incorporates numerous Sunni perspectives. Furthermore, Zaydis reject the mystical and metaphysical doctrines characteristic of Twelver Shia Islam, such as the belief in the twelfth “Hidden Imam.”
In alignment with Shi’a doctrine, Zaydis maintain that Islamic leadership should ideally belong to the direct descendants of Muhammad, but a defining distinction of Zaydi theology is its acceptance of the early Sunni Caliphates, a stance that sets Zaydis apart from other Shi’a groups. The Zaydi position holds an intriguing middle ground between the Sunnis and other Shi’a.
Yemen’s 20th-century history was defined by systemic instability, civil conflict, political assassinations and frequent coups. A primary driver of this volatility has been the enduring friction and mutual distrust between the Yemeni Zaydi population, which makes up 35 to 45 percent of the country, and Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has consistently funded and supported various Yemeni factions to counter Zaydi influence.
In 1994, Hussein al-Houthi established Ansar Allah as a Zaydi Shi’a revivalist movement. Drawing ideological inspiration from the Iranian government, the group adopted an explicitly anti-Western and anti-Israel doctrine. In 2004, a government attempt to arrest al-Houthi ignited a decade-long insurgency against the Yemeni state, which eventually escalated into direct border clashes with Saudi forces. In 2014 the Houthis seized control of the capital, Sana’a, leading to military intervention by a Saudi-led coalition. Today, the breach between the Saudis and Houthis is wider than ever.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi oil fields and even Riyadh’s international airport in response to Saudi attacks on military and civilian infrastructure in Yemen. The Houthis say they’ve carried out these attacks “so that the world understands that airports, seaports, wedding and mourning halls, hospitals and markets in Yemen are civilian facilities that must not be targeted or harmed—and that the same rules that apply to these facilities in Yemen must also apply to their counterparts everywhere else.”
These developments have forced the hand of Washington. In September, U.S. officials reportedly met with a delegation of Houthis at the U.S. Embassy in Muscat, Oman, and entered into a conditional, secret understanding regarding shipping in the Red Sea.
The Houthis agreed to allow safe passage of U.S. military and commercial shipping through the Red Sea on the condition that the United States does not attack them. This remarkable development threatens a rift between Washington, DC and Riyadh, which had expected the United States to assist in striking the Houthis.
Iran and the Houthis have cornered the Saudi oil trade, restricting exports. The United States was reluctant to act against the Houthis as it cannot afford a shutdown of the Red Sea passage, and it is militarily stretched after constant activity in the Strait of Hormuz. This strategic move by the Houthis is having the desired effect, a fragmentation of relations between the United States and Saudi Arabia.
As we went to press, the conflict is escalating rapidly. Regional tensions have intensified following the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, on Oct. 10, 2026, that killed 12, including one American. President Trump condemned the attack and indicated he is reconsidering joining the Saudi-led operation. But translating rhetoric into military action is a big leap with myriad consequences. Regardless of their strategic intentions, the key stakeholders in this conflict are increasingly drawn into this geopolitical quagmire.
A riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma indeed. In this extraordinary game of geopolitical chess, the Houthis are no pawns. The key to understanding their actions may be found in the realm of their own national interest.
P. Bruce McLaren, Ph.D. (University of Sydney), is an archaeologist and historian who has worked extensively in the Middle East and Central Asia, with a focus on military architecture and warfare. He is the author of three books, including a study of the history of conflict in Syria entitled The Plain of Dead Cities: A Syrian Tale (2015).

articles.title: As Houthis encircle Taiz, Yemen's Saudi-backed gov't faces disaster - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: As Houthis encircle Taiz, Yemen's Saudi-backed gov't faces disaster  Responsible StatecraftYemeni City of Taiz Running Out of Essentials as Houthis Close in  The New York TimesHouthis attack besieged city in Yemen that U.N. says is at ‘grave risk’  NBC NewsYemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises  Al JazeeraYemen war continues to force families from homes amid hunger and disease  UN News
articles.full_text:
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, endured a siege from 2015 to 2017. Today, it is encircled again.
The World Food Program says it cannot reach more than 600,000 people in and around the city. The International Organization for Migration counts over 200,000 people displaced since the Houthi offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast launched in September.
Why this city, and why now? The Houthis, formally known as the Ansar Allah movement, draw their strength from the Zaydi Shia highlands of the north. Critics say their governing ideology rests on the belief that the right to rule belongs to sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Mohammad, a lineage to which the Houthi family itself belongs. The Houthis have long denied seeking to restore the Imamate, but in Taiz, which has for a decade resisted Houthi encroachment, that denial finds few believers.
Taiz has a long history of political activism and hostility to the idea of religious hereditary rule. Its poets and journalists supplied much of the dissident energy that toppled the Imamate in 1962, and its streets were one of the centers of the 2011 uprising against then-President Ali Abdallah Saleh. This gives the governorate symbolic weight disproportionate to its size.
Moreover, Taiz is significant for its geography. It sits at the hinge between the Red Sea coast and the southern highlands that shelter the city of Aden, currently the administrative capital of Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, which the Houthis struck last week with missiles. Houthi control of the surrounding mountains would make the government’s counteroffensive around the Bab al-Mandab strait far harder to sustain.
That counteroffensive, known as Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” was announced on October 5 by President Rashad al-Alimi, a native of the Taiz governorate who chairs the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, the body that leads Yemen’s internationally-recognized government.
The stated aim of the counteroffensive is to recover the whole country from the Houthis, the capital Sana’a included. So far, it seems to have stalled in its second week.
Government forces, under heavy Saudi air cover, have retaken ground around Bab al-Mandab and Dhubab. But Mokha, the coastal prize the Houthis seized in September, remains in Houthi hands.
The Houthis hold a contiguous area and can shift forces and materiel between fronts with relative ease. Their opponents consist of numerous factions fighting under the government umbrella, each of which answers to different commanders with different political projects. When the west coast collapsed in September, Tareq Saleh, who heads the National Resistance Forces that held the coast, withdrew to Aden, where southern units initially refused his men entry. The southerners' wariness stems from the role Saleh's uncle, then president, played in the 1994 civil war, when northern forces overran the south and crushed their bid for independence.
Indeed, Yemen’s civil war was already heavily shaped by external forces. Today, it has grown even more tightly bound to the wider U.S.- Iran war.
Since July, the Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping and turned their arsenal on the kingdom itself. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been attacked multiple times this month, with 13 killed and over 300 wounded.
The Houthis also hit Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran last week, with fire spreading across several floors. Reuters estimates Saudi crude output ran below 7 million barrels a day for most of the first six months of the U.S.-Iran war, leading to $50 billion in lost revenue at current prices. The International Monetary Fund expects the Saudi economy to shrink by 3.3% this year.
Riyadh’s response has been aggressive in substance toward the Houthis but restrained in tone toward Iran, the movement's primary patron. Saudi Arabia says it has carried out waves of air and missile strikes on Houthi territory, yet Saudi officials largely stop short of naming Tehran.
The reticence is probably deliberate. Riyadh has every reason to preserve room for a deal between Washington and Tehran that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and hopefully end attacks from Iran and Iran-aligned groups on Saudi soil. Iran is also the outside power with the most influence over the Houthis. If Tehran chose to press them to de-escalate, that could create space for a Saudi-Houthi ceasefire and talks.
Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy.
In the meantime, the kingdom has few viable options to escalate pressure on the Houthis, who set the tempo of escalation.
Turkey and Pakistan have activated the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, but both describe their roles as defensive. Egypt’s President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi on Saturday asked parliament for authority to militarily support the kingdom, but stressed that “we are speaking only about defense.”
President Donald Trump recently noted that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and suggested he may ask Turkey to get more involved. Yet, with midterm elections looming on November 3, a war on Iran that has dragged on for eight months without settlement, and oil prices climbing, another American campaign in Yemen is the last thing the White House wants.
Riyadh, short of options, has yet to offer a comprehensive strategy beyond punitive airstrikes on the Houthis and support for its Yemeni partners’ counteroffensive, which is faring poorly, as the siege of Taiz makes clear.
The best clue to official thinking is a recent column by Abdulrahman al-Rashed, a former editor of Asharq al-Awsat and a well-connected Saudi commentator. He answers those who argue that the world should simply negotiate with the Houthis, as it has with other rulers of Sana’a.
The Houthi project, he argues, “is fundamentally at odds with the very idea of the state.” He describes how the Houthis have used all concessions and pauses to re-arm and wage war, calling the group “yet another Iranian proxy in the region, not the nucleus of an ordinary Yemeni system of government.”
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman appears to share this view that the Houthis are not a group to be accommodated. Chairing the cabinet on October 13, he declared that the “terrorist Houthi militia will face the consequences of its heinous crimes and attacks.”
Tehran’s position, meanwhile, has been contradictory. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei says Iran will help mediate if both sides ask and denies any role in Yemeni operations. Yet numerous investigative reports demonstrate that Iranian advisers and intelligence actively enabled the Houthi capture of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
Though Saudi Arabia has not responded to the mediation offer, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, Afrah al-Zouba, rejected it, calling Iran a “party to the war against the Yemeni people.”
This is not a surprising response. Iran’s own hardline press betrays official neutrality, running headlines that celebrate Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities.
One report in Kayhan, whose editor-in-chief is selected by Iran's supreme leader, refers to the Houthis as the “Yemeni resistance” and frames war in Yemen as a “twelve-year aggression of the Saudi-American coalition.” Moreover, an adviser to the parliamentary speaker, one of the key negotiators with the U.S., wrote that Iran would use “tools in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb and beyond” to keep oil prices elevated.
More telling is the extent to which Tehran has adopted the Houthi vocabulary. Iranian officials describe the Houthis as “Yemen’s armed forces,” overlooking the Saudi-backed government that holds Yemen’s U.N. seat, and call Saudi restrictions on flights and ports in Houthi-held territory a “blockade.” Riyadh sees those measures as the enforcement of a U.N.-backed arms embargo and as support for Yemen’s recognized government, whose current executive council took shape under Saudi sponsorship in 2022, after Riyadh pressed the previous president to step aside and transfer his powers to the newly created governing council.
Iran thus arrives with its position on the central questions already fixed, rendering its mediation offers largely hollow. Any Saudi move to the table would look like a concession to the Houthis’ and Tehran’s framing. That makes talks harder for Riyadh, even if it wanted them.

articles.full_text:
Concern comes as Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend against Houthi attacks.
The Trump administration now assesses that Houthi attacks pose a broad, escalating threat to Americans in the Middle East, prompting an unprecedented decision by the State Department to issue urgent warnings about the Iranian-backed rebel group across a dozen countries in the region, U.S. officials told ABC News.
While the department has been notifying U.S. nationals in Saudi Arabia about the risk of Houthi attacks for weeks, U.S. embassies in Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and the UAE issued coordinated security alerts on Sunday, advising Americans that hostilities involving Houthi militants "have the potential to escalate rapidly" beyond areas that have been impacted so far.
The U.S. mission to Yemen and its virtual embassy for Iran also issued identical messages.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance. These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," State Department Deputy Assistant Secretary for Press Edgar Vasquez said in a statement to ABC News.
The heightened concern comes as Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend against deadly missile and drone strikes on energy and aviation targets, such as an attack on Riyadh's main international airport earlier this month that claimed that killed 13 people, including an American citizen.
The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia has been issuing near-daily alerts to Americans traveling in the country, advising on Monday that they should "be aware of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations, and travel disruptions" and "take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia."
Saudi Arabia has also displayed signs of growing alarm, postponing a major annual investment conference commonly referred to as "Davos in the Desert" due to the security environment.
While Saudi-led forces have carried out significant air and ground operations against the Houthis in Yemen, these campaigns have not curtailed incoming attacks. On Monday, a spokesperson for the rebel group claimed it launched multiple strikes against Saudi targets.
Riyadh is actively trying to court regional support for its fight against the Houthis, and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman previously appealed to President Trump for support.
The U.S. has been providing Saudi Arabia with significant targeting assistance and intelligence support. But so far Trump has declined to order direct U.S. military intervention, as sources say the administration has been wary of opening a second front in the Middle East while the conflict with Iran remains unsettled.
Last week, Trump told ABC News that the Houthis were "behaving very badly," but did not say whether he would change his mind on ordering strikes against the rebel group.
The Houthis are a Shiite political and military organization that took form as an opposition force to the Yemeni government.
In 2011, the Houthis played a major role in sparking the Yemeni Revolution, which was born out of a wave of anti-government protests and uprisings known as the Arab Spring.
The revolution forced a transfer of power, but the Houthis were displeased with the newly installed leaders and in 2014 the group took control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, prompting an ongoing civil war that has ravaged the country.
A Saudi-led coalition first intervened in the conflict in 2015 with the stated goal of restoring the former rulers to power. A UN-brokered truce was reached in 2022, resulting in relative calm until mid-2026.
Amid broader regional tensions, the Houthis resumed attacks against Saudi Arabia in July. In September, the group launched a ground campaign that resulted in significant initial territorial gains across western Yemen, triggering a counter-offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
