articles.title: Iran vows retaliation to any US attack, rejects no-response deal claims
articles.summary: Iran warned Tuesday it will retaliate against any U.S. military strike, dismissing claims that Washington messaged Tehran expecting it to refrain from responding. Speaking at his w...
articles.full_text:
Iran warned Tuesday it will retaliate against any U.S. military strike, dismissing claims that Washington messaged Tehran expecting it to refrain from responding.
Speaking at his weekly press conference, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei described suggestions that the U.S. could attack Iran without retaliation as an "illusion."
He rejected claims Washington had sent a message urging Iran to refrain from responding to a potential U.S. attack.
Baghaei said Tehran had demonstrated it would answer any military strike, adding that "If our response is not stronger, it will certainly be equal."
The spokesperson stressed that the era of the U.S. attacking and withdrawing without consequences was over.
His remarks came in response to claims of a possible U.S. attack on Pickaxe Mountain (Kuh-e Kolang) in Iran.
Baghaei also warned that Iran remained prepared for another Israeli attack, saying the country was not experiencing peace.
Responding to media reports that Israeli officials had discussed another war against Iran with regional parties, he said Tehran was constantly assessing potential threats.
"We live with this possibility and face it day and night," he said, citing the continuing U.S. naval blockade and threats against Iran as reasons for military readiness.
He said Iranian forces had learned from the past two years and were prepared to repel any assault.
Baghaei said Tehran had not entered nuclear negotiations with Washington and thus had no details of such talks to discuss with Russia or other countries.
"We have not entered nuclear negotiations with Washington to discuss their details with other parties," he said.
He rejected speculation that Iran had softened its positions on the nuclear issue, stressing Tehran remained committed to its principles and national interests.
The spokesperson said Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s visit to Tehran was part of regular consultations between the two countries.
He noted the visit had been planned for months and aimed to discuss bilateral relations and regional and international developments.
Baghaei said discussions covered the Caucasus, Europe, the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program.
He said Russia had played an important role in previous negotiations that led to the 2015 nuclear agreement and continued to offer to help reduce tensions.
Baghaei also dismissed remarks by U.S. officials regarding Iran’s relations with Russia and China, saying Tehran would continue developing ties with both countries regardless of Washington's rhetoric.
He said Iran's cooperation with Moscow and Beijing was based on mutual interests, stressing Tehran understood both countries pursued their own national priorities.
Referring to U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks, Baghaei said Iranian officials would not engage with such rhetoric, adding sometimes it was better to let others remain in their "illusions."
Baghaei said Tehran would continue pursuing diplomatic opportunities despite its longstanding distrust of Washington.
He accused the U.S. of repeatedly violating its commitments, including since its withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018.
However, he stressed Iran's diplomatic institutions could not abandon negotiations solely because of previous experiences.
"If there is even the slightest possibility diplomacy can prevent an escalation of tensions, we must pursue that path," he said.
Baghaei added Iran's priority remained protecting its national interests and security, whether through diplomacy or military defense.
The spokesperson said a recent message received from the U.S. was "insufficient and incomplete," adding Tehran had already communicated its position to Washington.
He said Iran's seven demands were neither new nor unreasonable, arguing they had already been included in the June understanding between the two countries.
Baghaei cited lifting the U.S. naval blockade and ending hostilities on all fronts among Tehran’s demands, describing them as legitimate and reasonable.
He said Washington needed to make a decision on these issues before diplomatic efforts could move forward.
Baghaei blamed continued U.S. military actions for insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz, calling on the United Nations to help address the situation.
Responding to a question regarding humanitarian shipments, including agricultural supplies and food production materials, he said Tehran had consistently supported efforts to facilitate humanitarian deliveries.
However, he argued the underlying causes of insecurity in the strategic waterway required addressing.
"The cause of insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is clear: the continuation of U.S. interventionist and aggressive actions," he said.
Baghaei urged the U.N. to take steps to prevent Washington from continuing what Tehran considers destabilizing actions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf.
The spokesperson also rejected a resolution adopted at an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) foreign ministers' meeting in Baghdad expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
He said Iran had formally opposed the resolution and did not consider it a valid OIC decision, citing what he called failure to follow the organization's procedural rules.
Baghaei said Tehran also prevented the inclusion of two paragraphs regarding Yemen in the meeting's final declaration, arguing their wording would deepen divisions among Muslim countries.
He said the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen should be resolved through dialogue and reconciliation rather than military force.
"The issue of Yemen cannot be resolved through force," he said.
Baghaei called on neighboring countries to prevent foreign powers from using their territory and military facilities to threaten or attack other states.
He said preventing such activities was essential to establishing lasting regional security and maintaining good-neighborly relations.
The spokesperson also accused Israel’s policies and territorial expansion of fueling regional instability.
He said the war in Gaza had not ended the suffering of Palestinians and reiterated Tehran’s criticism of U.S. and European support for Israel.

articles.title: Rubio puts trade deal, Venezuelan oil at center of India visit - PRESS Insider
articles.summary: Rubio puts trade deal, Venezuelan oil at center of India visit  PRESS Insider
articles.full_text:
The US secretary of state says a trade agreement is nearly complete as Washington presses India to expand energy purchases and looks to Reliance Industries for help easing global oil supply pressures
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington and New Delhi are close to finalizing a long-delayed trade agreement, while pushing for greater energy cooperation that could see Reliance Industries Ltd refine more Venezuelan crude and potentially invest in oil production in the South American country.
Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai on Tuesday, 20 October, for his second visit to India this year, held talks with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on trade, defense, technology and regional security.
He was scheduled to visit Reliance’s Jamnagar refining complex in Gujarat on Wednesday, 21 October, where discussions with chairman Mukesh Ambani are expected to focus on oil supplies and investment.
The visit comes days after US President Donald Trump granted a temporary waiver from potential punitive tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil, removing an immediate obstacle to a trade agreement that has faced repeated delays over tariffs, market access and India’s energy relationship with Moscow.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
He said only a small number of issues remained unresolved and expected the negotiations to conclude shortly.
In an interview with The Indian Express, Rubio put the agreement’s progress at 99%, saying the remaining differences largely concerned specific words and phrases. No final agreement or signing date has been announced.
The negotiations have become an important test of whether the two governments can contain their commercial disputes while maintaining cooperation on defense, technology and security in the Indo-Pacific.
Trade talks near the finish line
India and the US have spent much of the past year negotiating a trade agreement against a backdrop of American tariff increases and disagreements over Russian energy imports.
A framework agreed in February eased some of the earlier trade friction, but negotiations remained difficult as Washington pressed for greater access to India’s market and New Delhi sought relief from American duties.
Rubio’s visit follows signs of renewed progress. US ambassador to India Sergio Gor said last week that negotiations were moving rapidly, with major parts of the proposed agreement already settled.
The remaining terms have not been made public. Nor is it clear how far the agreement will protect Indian exporters from future American tariff measures or what concessions India has made on access to its domestic market.
Preferential tariff treatment would improve the competitiveness of Indian exporters, while easier access to the Indian market could benefit American manufacturers and suppliers, analysts said.
Washington has also been pressing India to buy more American energy, technology and defense equipment.
Rubio’s assessment suggests the negotiations have moved beyond their most difficult stage, although the absence of a signed agreement leaves companies without certainty about the final terms.
Russian oil remains a concern
The talks have been complicated by India’s continued purchases of Russian crude, which expanded after Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russian supplies offered Indian refiners an alternative to more expensive crude from other markets, but the trade became a recurring source of tension with Washington as the US sought to reduce Russia’s oil revenue.
Trump’s decision last week to waive potential punitive tariffs gave India some relief and created more room for negotiations.
The waiver, however, is temporary. Washington is expected to review the matter over 60 days, leaving open the possibility that pressure over Russian energy purchases could return.
The decision has also drawn criticism from American lawmakers who argue that the administration has been too accommodating toward Moscow.
Rubio defended the need to balance economic and geopolitical considerations. He acknowledged India’s efforts to diversify its oil supplies, while recognizing that the country continues to buy substantial volumes of Russian crude.
For New Delhi, the difficulty lies in securing enough competitively priced oil without becoming excessively dependent on a supplier exposed to American sanctions.
For Washington, the challenge is to encourage diversification while avoiding further disruption to energy markets already strained by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Why Washington wants Reliance to process Venezuelan oil
The commercial focus of Rubio’s visit is expected to become clearer in Jamnagar, home to Reliance’s two large refineries with a combined processing capacity of about 1.4 million barrels per day.
The complex can process heavy and high-sulfur crude grades that many other refineries cannot handle economically. That capability makes Reliance an important prospective buyer of Venezuela’s unusually heavy oil.
Rubio said Washington intends to encourage the Indian company to increase its purchases and refining of Venezuelan crude as more of the country’s production becomes available.
“We will talk about (refining more Venezuelan crude) tomorrow with Reliance,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday.
He also indicated that discussions could extend to Reliance participating directly in oil production in Venezuela, an option previously considered but not implemented.
Reliance already imports Venezuelan crude, but does not currently operate oil-producing assets in the country.
The renewed interest follows major political changes in Venezuela and Washington’s efforts to bring more of its oil to international markets.
Venezuelan crude could provide Indian refiners with another supply option while helping Washington reduce the pressure created by restricted Russian exports and instability in the Middle East.
There are limits to how quickly this could happen.
Venezuela’s production infrastructure requires investment, and its heavy crude needs specialized handling and refining. Higher output would also depend on commercial terms, transport availability and a sufficiently stable policy environment.
For Reliance, decisions on Venezuelan investments would need to make commercial sense beyond the immediate diplomatic interest. No new supply contract or production investment has been announced.
UAE joins discussions on energy security
The energy agenda extended beyond the bilateral relationship. Jaishankar and Rubio held a trilateral meeting in Mumbai with UAE deputy prime minister and foreign minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
The ministers discussed regional energy security, connectivity and economic cooperation at a time when conflict in the Middle East has raised concerns about oil supplies and shipping routes.
The UAE is an important energy supplier to India and a major commercial partner of both countries. Its participation brought a Gulf producer directly into discussions between two of the world’s major energy-consuming economies.
The meeting also showed how India’s energy diplomacy now reaches beyond the question of where it buys crude. Disruptions to oil production, shipping, insurance and regional trade routes can affect India’s import costs, its current account and the availability of fuel across the economy.
A sustained increase in energy prices would raise the dollar cost of India’s imports and potentially add pressure on the rupee.
Defense, technology and the China question
Trade and oil dominated Rubio’s public comments, but his discussions with Jaishankar covered a wider strategic relationship. The ministers reviewed opportunities to expand cooperation in defense, technology, energy and people-to-people ties, along with regional developments.
The two countries have increasingly linked their commercial relationship to security interests, particularly the need to diversify supply chains, protect critical technologies and strengthen their positions in the Indo-Pacific.
India is an important partner in the Quad, alongside the US, Japan and Australia, a grouping whose agenda includes maritime security, technology and regional cooperation.
China remains an important strategic consideration for both Washington and New Delhi, although India has consistently maintained its own foreign policy priorities rather than entering a formal military alliance with the US.
Rubio has sought to reassure New Delhi that Washington continues to regard the relationship as a long-term priority. Yet the durability of that partnership will also depend on how the two governments handle differences over trade, immigration and relations with other countries, analysts said.
Political sensitivities persist
Rubio’s decision to hold talks in Mumbai rather than New Delhi attracted criticism from Indian opposition figures before the visit.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was not scheduled to meet him on this trip, unlike his earlier visit in May.
The choice of Mumbai placed the emphasis on India’s financial and commercial center, with the subsequent visit to Jamnagar giving the trip a substantial industrial component.
No official explanation was given for omitting New Delhi from the itinerary. Questions about Washington’s relationship with Pakistan have also persisted in India, alongside concerns over US visa restrictions and immigration policy.
In his interview to The Indian Express, Rubio sought to address some of those concerns and described the bilateral relationship in positive terms. The administration’s recent decisions on tariffs and Russian oil, however, illustrate the extent to which cooperation remains subject to broader American policy calculations.
Rubio also paid tribute to the victims of the November 2008 terrorist attacks in Mumbai at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel.
At a reception marking 250 years of American independence, Jaishankar thanked him

articles.title: Amid West Asia Tensions, India And UAE Push To Deepen Trade, Energy And Defence Ties During Deputy PM Al Nahyan's Visit - ETV Bharat
articles.summary: Amid West Asia Tensions, India And UAE Push To Deepen Trade, Energy And Defence Ties During Deputy PM Al Nahyan's Visit  ETV Bharat
articles.full_text:
UAE Deputy PM Sheikh Abdullah Bin Zayed Al Nahyan concluded his two-day official visit to India on Tuesday, further solidifying ties between the two nations.
New Delhi: Amid prevailing concerns over the situation in West Asia, India and the UAE have reaffirmed their commitment to closer strategic ties, with focus on trade, energy security, defence and technology.
The development comes during UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah Bin Zayed Al Nahyan's two-day visit to India, where he held delegation-level talks with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and reviewed the overarching progress of the India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
In a post on X, the Office of the UAE Minister of Foreign Affairs stated, "Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed held an expanded meeting with Dr S Jaishankar, Minister of External Affairs, in Mumbai, where they discussed new opportunities to enhance the comprehensive strategic and economic partnership between UAE and India, and to expand the horizons of bilateral cooperation in vital sectors, in support of the two countries' aspirations for further growth and prosperity."
According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), both ministers "expressed satisfaction at the steady progress achieved across key areas of cooperation, including trade, investment, energy, defence, technology and people-to-people ties".
The discussions also referenced recent high-level diplomatic exchanges, with both leaders noting the "recent productive visit of EAM to Abu Dhabi and Ras Al Khaimah". Beyond bilateral issues, Jaishankar and Sheikh Abdullah "exchanged perspectives on regional and global issues of mutual interest and agreed to continue their close and regular consultations".

articles.title: India, US, UAE hold trilateral talks on energy security, trade and connectivity in Mumbai - NewsDrum
articles.summary: India, US, UAE hold trilateral talks on energy security, trade and connectivity in Mumbai  NewsDrum
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: India, the United States and the United Arab Emirates held trilateral talks in Mumbai on Tuesday, focusing on regional energy security, trade, technology and connectivity at a time when the conflict in West Asia has disrupted global oil supplies and created fresh concerns over international shipping routes.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan participated in the meeting, which also examined opportunities for cooperation in artificial intelligence, investment and regional economic integration.
The meeting brought together three countries with substantial economic and energy interests in the Gulf, as Washington seeks to ease pressure on global oil markets while India looks to safeguard energy supplies and strengthen trade relationships amid continuing geopolitical uncertainty.
"Held a trilateral meeting with DPM and FM UAE Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. A useful exchange of perspectives on energy, connectivity and contemporary developments," Jaishankar wrote on X.
Rubio described the meeting as an opportunity to advance the countries' economic interests while addressing regional energy concerns.
"It was great to meet with Indian External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan to discuss regional energy security and advance our shared economic priorities," he said.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said the three countries had opportunities to translate their existing relationships into practical cooperation.
"The US, India, and UAE have real opportunities to advance cooperation on energy, trade, technology, and regional connectivity," Gor wrote on X, describing the discussions as an effort to turn close diplomatic ties into concrete results.
According to a statement issued by the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the ministers examined opportunities for cooperation across trade, investment, technology and artificial intelligence, with the objective of strengthening economic integration and supporting sustainable development.
The three leaders also exchanged views on regional and international developments, including ongoing efforts to strengthen security and stability.
Sheikh Abdullah emphasised that the UAE's strategic partnerships with India and the United States continued to expand and that the three countries had opportunities to deepen cooperation in sectors supporting their respective development priorities.
UAE Minister of State for International Cooperation Reem bint Ebrahim Al Hashimy also attended the trilateral meeting.
Energy security takes centre stage amid West Asia conflict
The discussions come against the backdrop of continuing disruptions to energy supplies from West Asia, where the conflict involving Iran and threats to shipping routes have increased pressure on oil markets and complicated the movement of crude oil, petroleum products and other essential commodities.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a substantial share of the world's seaborne oil trade normally passes, has remained a major source of concern, while recent attacks by Houthi militants on Saudi energy facilities have added to uncertainty over regional supplies.
India, which depends heavily on imported crude oil, has been seeking to diversify its sources of supply while maintaining access to affordable energy from existing partners, including Russia and countries in the Gulf.
The UAE remains an important energy supplier to India and a major trading and investment partner, making coordination between New Delhi and Abu Dhabi particularly significant during periods of regional instability.
Earlier on Tuesday, during his bilateral meeting with Sheikh Abdullah, Jaishankar expressed concern over the situation in the Gulf and reiterated India's support for diplomatic efforts to restore stability.
"The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern. We will continue to work together and support all efforts to promote dialogue and diplomacy," Jaishankar said.
He also underlined the importance of maintaining uninterrupted international commerce.
"We continue to support free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertilisers," the minister said, while thanking the UAE leadership for ensuring the welfare of the Indian community living in the Emirates.
Approximately 4.5 million Indians live in the UAE, making their safety and economic well-being another important consideration in India's approach to developments in West Asia.
Rubio says India-US trade agreement is close
The trilateral engagement followed separate talks between Jaishankar and Rubio, during which the two sides reviewed bilateral cooperation in trade, energy, defence, technology and people-to-people relations.
"Pleased to meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Mumbai today. We shared views on further advancement of our ties, focusing on trade, energy, technology, defence and people-to-people ties. Also exchanged views on regional developments," Jaishankar said.
Rubio said the discussions had reaffirmed the importance of strengthening the India-US strategic partnership, particularly in energy security and defence cooperation.
The meeting took place as both governments seek to conclude a bilateral trade agreement after months of difficult negotiations over tariffs, market access and India's energy purchases from Russia.
Speaking to reporters in Mumbai, Rubio indicated that an agreement was approaching completion.
"We're very, very close. I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement," Rubio said, adding that only a small number of outstanding issues remained to be resolved.
The United States imposed tariffs of up to 50% on most Indian goods in August 2025 following disagreements over trade and Russian oil purchases, although the tariff rate was subsequently reduced to 18% under a framework agreed in February 2026.
Negotiations on the broader trade agreement have continued since then, with Indian officials seeking tariff treatment comparable to competing manufacturing economies.
Earlier in October, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the negotiations as having plateaued, while Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal subsequently indicated that the first phase of the agreement was in its final stages.
Rubio's latest remarks suggest that Washington expects the remaining differences to be resolved soon, although neither government announced a final agreement following Tuesday's discussions.
Rubio to visit Jamnagar refinery for energy talks
Energy cooperation is also expected to feature prominently during Rubio's scheduled visit to Reliance Industries' Jamnagar refining complex in Gujarat on Wednesday.
Rubio said Washington was interested in exploring opportunities for Reliance to process larger quantities of Venezuelan crude oil, which could help increase refined petroleum supplies at a time of pressure on global markets.
The Jamnagar complex, operated by Mukesh Ambani-led Reliance Industries, is the world's largest refining complex and has the technical capability to process heavy crude grades, including those produced in Venezuela.
Speaking to reporters in Mumbai, Rubio said the United States had previously discussed the possibility of increasing Venezuelan crude processing with Reliance and intended to examine the obstacles holding back such arrangements.
Washington has also acknowledged that India cannot immediately replace its existing oil suppliers, particularly Russia, given the scale of its energy requirements and the difficulties involved in shifting international supply chains.
Rubio has said India has already made progress in diversifying its energy portfolio and that the United States wants to support further diversification.
The Trump administration recently paused certain sanctions affecting Russian oil sales amid concerns over global supply disruptions, providing temporary relief to countries dependent on those imports.
Rubio's Jamnagar visit is expected to include discussions on energy cooperation and engagement with business representatives, although no new crude supply agreement has been announced so far.

articles.title: Israel tech sector 2026: Emerging growth hurdles - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Israel tech sector 2026: Emerging growth hurdles  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Israel’s high-tech industry stands at a critical crossroads. The sector that drives nearly a fifth of the nation’s economy now confronts a complex web of global pressures, domestic shifts, and unprecedented possibilities. Investors are watching closely, start-ups are adapting rapidly, and the world continues to follow Israel’s technology ecosystem. This moment demands strategic thinking, flexibility, and decisive action. One platform associated with strategic decision-making and calculated choices is Rocket Play casino AUS, where participants weigh different options and outcomes. In a broader sense, Israel’s technology sector faces a similarly dynamic environment, where timing, expertise, and adaptability can shape long-term results.
The landscape has transformed dramatically since the early 2000s, when Israel first earned its "start-up Nation" nickname. Today, the ecosystem faces headwinds from global economic uncertainty, shifts in venture capital flows, and evolving geopolitical realities. Yet opportunity remains strong. Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, climate tech, and quantum computing are opening new frontiers. The question isn’t whether Israel will remain relevant. It’s how the nation will adapt, reinvent, and lead.
Key facts: Numbers that define the moment
The following statistics paint a clear picture of where Israel’s technology sector stands and where it is heading.
- Israeli tech companies raised $8.2 billion in 2025, a 25% decline from 2024’s $11 billion peak, according to the Israel Innovation Authority.
- The sector employs approximately 400,000 people, representing 9.2% of the national workforce, with an average salary of $8,500 per month.
- Cybersecurity exports reached $17.5 billion in 2025, solidifying Israel’s position as the second-largest global exporter in this field.
- By 2026, experts project that AI-related start-ups will account for 35% of all new Israeli tech ventures, up from 22% in 2023.
- The number of active tech companies in Israel exceeds 7,500, with over 60% founded after 2019.
- Research and development spending in the private sector hit 5.6% of GDP in 2025, the highest ratio among OECD nations.
- A staggering 92% of Israeli tech founders report difficulties securing late-stage funding, pushing many toward strategic acquisitions or overseas expansion.
Talent wars and the battle for human capital
The competition for skilled engineers has intensified significantly. Global tech giants continue to open research centers in Tel Aviv, Haifa, and Jerusalem, attracting local talent with compensation packages that smaller start-ups often cannot match. Microsoft, Google, and Nvidia employ thousands of Israeli developers, contributing to a widening gap between established technology companies and smaller ventures.
Meanwhile, universities produce roughly 12,000 engineering graduates annually, a number that falls short of industry demand by nearly 40%.
The military remains an important source of technical and leadership expertise. Elite units such as Unit 8200 and Talpiot produce graduates with strong technical and organizational skills. These veterans often launch ventures within months of completing service, bringing discipline and mission-focused thinking to their companies.
However, mandatory reserve duty can disrupt business continuity. start-ups may lose key personnel for extended periods, affecting development schedules and investor confidence. Some companies have responded by incorporating reserve obligations into workforce planning and project management.
Remote work has also reshaped recruitment strategies. Israeli firms increasingly hire developers from Eastern Europe, India, and Latin America, creating distributed teams that operate across multiple time zones. This approach helps alleviate local talent shortages but can introduce communication and coordination challenges. Successful companies invest heavily in internal tools, documentation practices, and cultural integration programs. Increasingly, global teams are viewed as a strategic advantage rather than a temporary solution.
Funding realities: From easy money to strategic patience
Venture capital flows have cooled considerably since the rapid expansion of 2021. Back then, start-ups secured funding with limited due diligence and increasingly ambitious valuations. Those conditions have changed. Investors now demand clearer revenue paths, realistic burn rates, and demonstrated product-market fit.
Seed rounds take longer to close, while Series A and B funding rounds face greater scrutiny. The era of growth-at-all-costs has given way to more disciplined capital allocation.
Government programs attempt to fill part of the funding gap. The Israel Innovation Authority offers grants for early-stage research, covering up to 50% of approved project costs. These funds help bridge the gap between prototype development and commercial viability. Yet bureaucratic delays remain a concern for founders. Application processing times average four months, which can be significant in a rapidly changing technology environment.
Some start-ups bypass government support entirely, instead turning to accelerators, angel networks, or corporate venture arms.
Exit strategies have also evolved. IPOs on NASDAQ remain attractive but demanding. Many companies now consider dual listings, mergers with special purpose acquisition companies, or strategic sales to multinational corporations. The acquisition route can provide earlier liquidity for investors and founders.
Recent deals include cybersecurity firm Axonius raising $200 million and AI chip designer NeuReality securing $70 million. These transactions demonstrate continued international interest in Israeli innovation despite broader economic uncertainty.
The regional factor: Geopolitics and market access
Israel’s geographic position creates both opportunities and obstacles. Normalization agreements with the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Morocco opened doors to Gulf markets. Trade in technology goods and services with these partners grew 400% since 2020.
Joint ventures in fintech, agricultural technology, and water management have expanded. The Abraham Accords created new channels for commercial cooperation, investment, and access to customers across the Middle East.
At the same time, security concerns persist. Cyberattacks on Israeli infrastructure increased 300% in 2025, according to the Israel National Cyber Directorate. This threat environment has also contributed to continued demand for cybersecurity expertise. Israeli firms develop advanced defenses and export solutions to governments and corporations worldwide.
The nation’s expertise in this field remains internationally recognized, with companies such as Check Point, Wiz, and CyberArk maintaining major positions in global cybersecurity markets.
Relations with Europe and Asia continue to deepen. Trade agreements with the European Union facilitate technology transfers and joint research initiatives. Asian markets, particularly India and China, show growing interest in Israeli innovation.
Indian conglomerates invest heavily in Israeli agritech and water solutions, while Chinese firms have focused on artificial intelligence and autonomous systems. These partnerships diversify revenue streams and reduce dependence on any single market.
Innovation hotspots: Where the next wave builds
Beyond Tel Aviv’s bustling start-up scene, new technology hubs are emerging across the country.
Beersheba has transformed into a major cybersecurity center, anchored by the CyberSpark innovation center and its proximity to IDF intelligence units. The city attracted over 100 companies and created 5,000 jobs in the sector.
Jerusalem’s biomedical cluster continues to expand, leveraging partnerships with Hadassah Medical Center and Hebrew University. Companies such as Teva and Medtronic maintain significant operations there, supporting an ecosystem of medical-device and pharmaceutical start-ups.
The Negev desert hosts experimental renewable-energy projects. Solar farms, green hydrogen facilities, and battery-storage systems are attracting international attention. Climate-tech start-ups raised $1.2 billion in 2025, reflecting growing global investment in sustainability.
Companies such as H2Pro and Electriq Global are developing technologies that could reshape energy markets. The desert environment provides useful testing conditions for solutions designed to operate under extreme conditions.
Haifa’s maritime and logistics sectors are also gaining momentum. Port automation, autonomous shipping, and supply-chain optimization are attracting investment from global shipping companies.
The city’s Technion Institute remains a major center for engineering education, producing graduates who go on to launch ventures across multiple technology fields. Northern Israel, once overshadowed by Tel Aviv, is increasingly establishing its own position within the country’s innovation ecosystem.
Conclusion: A long-term outlook
Israel’s technology sector is navigating a period of significant change with characteristic resilience. The challenges are substantial: Talent shortages, funding constraints, geopolitical tensions, and global competition. Yet the fundamentals remain strong.
A culture of innovation, world-class research institutions, and a strong entrepreneurial tradition continue to shape the country’s technology ecosystem. The next decade will favor organizations that adapt, diversify, and think beyond conventional boundaries.
Long-term success will require patience, strategic vision, efficient resource allocation, and the ability to respond quickly to changing conditions. Israel’s technology sector is entering its next chapter, with emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, climate technology, and quantum computing likely to play an increasingly important role.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's official visit includes Qatar from Oct. 18 to 20, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from Oct. 20 to 22.
Photos via PM Wong's Facebook by MDDI/Sean Koh
Singapore and Qatar plan to upgrade their bilateral ties to a Strategic Partnership, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) in an Oct. 19 statement.
It added that both countries agreed to work towards elevating relations in a meeting on the same day with both countries' ministers and senior officials in attendance.
Co-chaired meeting
This comes amid Singapore's Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong's official visits to Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from Oct. 18 to 22.
On Oct. 19 in Doha, PM Wong and Tamim Bin Hamad Al Thani, the Emir of Qatar and its head of state, co-chaired the High-Level Joint Committee's (HLJC) ninth meeting.
This marked the first time that the HLJC was co-chaired by the leaders of both countries in its 20-year history, with both leaders reaffirming the warm and longstanding relations between Singapore and Qatar, the MFA statement added.
At the meeting, the leaders of both countries welcomed the continued growth of bilateral cooperation in areas including trade and investment, energy, and defence, both nations' HLJC said in a joint post-meeting statement.
The statement added that Qatar will become Singapore's second Strategic Partner in the Middle East, with the other being Saudi Arabia.
AI, defence
At the meeting, the leaders welcomed the growing cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), digitalisation, and emerging technologies.
They also encouraged cooperation among government agencies, research institutions, academia, and the private sector in AI, digital government, cybersecurity, data, innovation, research and development, and emerging technologies.
LNG
According to the joint statement, the leaders welcomed the renewal of the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between QatarEnergy and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry of Singapore on Cooperation in Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) and Low-Carbon Technology.
"The MOU underscores both sides' commitment to facilitating stable LNG procurement supply chains and energy security, especially in light of recent market developments," the statement read.
Concern over Middle East situation
At the meeting, the leaders also expressed serious concern over the situation in the Middle East, the HLJC statement noted.
They commended Qatar's sustained diplomatic efforts to facilitate dialogue and de-escalation in the region, emphasising the importance of upholding navigational rights and freedoms in accordance with international law, in particular the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
It ensures that international shipping, including in the Strait of Hormuz, remains open, safe and secure.
Small states
After arriving in Doha on Oct. 18, PM Wong met Qatar's Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who hosted him to an official dinner.
On Oct. 19, Emir Sheikh Tamim received PM Wong at Doha's Royal Court, welcoming him with a ceremony and hosting him to lunch.
PM Wong had visited the Qatar Foundation that morning, where he met Vice Chairperson Sheikha Hind Bint Hamad Al Thani and exchanged views on education, research and innovation.
In an Oct. 19 Facebook post, PM Wong said that as "Singapore prepares to chair the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2027, we look forward to deepening ASEAN–Qatar ties, as well as strengthening cooperation between ASEAN and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)".
He noted that "Singapore and Qatar are both small states navigating an increasingly troubled world".
"We share a strong interest in keeping our economies open, strengthening our resilience, and building a more secure and prosperous future for our peoples," he said.
"His Highness last visited Singapore in 2017, and I look forward to welcoming him back soon!"
The leaders had agreed to convene the 10th HLJC meeting in Singapore at a mutually convenient time, which the joint statement said was to be determined through diplomatic channels.
PM Wong will depart Qatar for the UAE on Oct. 20 for the second leg of his official visits.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance declined Monday to back Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's reelection bid, distancing himself from President Donald Trump's endorsement of the Israeli leader just a day earlier.
"The president has the most influential endorsement in American or international political history,” Vance said during an interview with journalist Mark Halperin.
"I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on the midterms,” Vance said, while traveling Monday to campaign for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley of North Carolina. "So, I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections.”
Vance has campaigned for a foreign leader - then-Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, last spring before the right-wing leader’s party lost that country's parliamentary election.
Vance’s deference to Trump on Netanyahu comes at an extraordinarily sensitive time for Jewish Americans and the U.S. alliance with Israel.
Republicans have been eager to portray Democrats, notably Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, as hostile toward Jews and Israel, while they deal with their own internal schisms.
Vance has faced skepticism from Jewish Republicans about his commitment to Jewish Americans and the U.S. alliance with Israel.
Last month, Vance spoke privately in Las Vegas to the Republican Jewish Coalition, a leading GOP group committed to advocating for a strong U.S. relationship with Israel and against antisemitism.
Vance left a positive impression on his RJC audience while stopping short of disavowing influential conservative podcast host Tucker Carlson.
Vance has faced general questions about his association with Carlson, a former Fox News host who faced backlash last year for interviewing antisemite Nick Fuentes on his podcast.
In June, Vance sharply criticized members of Israel’s government for opposing Trump’s efforts to resolve the war with Iran.
In July, Vance said elements of the Israeli government had tried to influence American sentiment to derail negotiations.
"There are some people within their system that we know beyond a shadow of a doubt are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” Vance said during an appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast.

Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip early Tuesday killed five Palestinians, including a married couple and two children, injured nine others, according to medical sources and witnesses.
The attacks occurred amid continued Israeli violations of a cease-fire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025.
Medics said an Israeli airstrike killed Akram Yassin and his wife Dina Abu Baker in an apartment in Gaza City.
The couple's bodies and four injured Palestinians, including three women, arrived at al-Shifa Hospital following the strike, a medical source told Türkiye's Anadolu Agency (AA).
Witnesses told AA that an Israeli helicopter fired at least one missile at their family home near al-Shifa Hospital, killing the couple and injuring others. The strike sparked a fire in the house that civil defense crews later extinguished, witnesses added.
Palestinians inspected the aftermath of the strike before gathering for the couple's funeral.
"We're supposed to be in a ceasefire period, but honestly, we are not seeing a ceasefire or anything. The war is still going on, assassinations are continuing, and the shelling has not stopped," said Mahmoud Yassin, whose brother was killed.
In Khan Younis, in the south, medics said a 17-year-old boy was killed by Israeli gunfire near the Qizan Al-Najar neighborhood.
A Palestinian child was also killed by Israeli army fire in the Wadi Gaza area in the central Gaza Strip, while another was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Zeitoun suburb east of Gaza City, taking Tuesday's death toll to at least five.
Five other Palestinians, including a woman and two children, were injured by Israeli army fire in Hamad City north of Khan Younis and areas south of the city.
In eastern Gaza City, the Israeli army shelled and fired heavily from military vehicles and quadcopter drones toward homes and tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Tuffah neighborhood.
Shelling and gunfire continued through the night. Witnesses heard several explosions as the Israeli army demolished homes and civilian structures in areas it controlled.
Israeli warships also fired toward Gaza City's northern coast, while military vehicles fired heavily toward the Sudaniya area in the northwestern Gaza Strip.
Witnesses said Israeli tanks fired heavily toward homes and tents for displaced people in central, southern and northern Khan Younis. The army also extensively demolished areas it controlled east of the city, witnesses added.
Earlier Monday, another Gazan was killed and three others were injured when an Israeli drone struck a gathering of civilians in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood in western Gaza City.
Another Palestinian also sustained moderate injuries when Israeli forces opened fire toward tents housing displaced people in the Nahr al-Bared camp area southwest of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
Israeli violations of the cease-fire agreement had killed 1,522 Palestinians and injured 5,421 others as of Monday, according to the latest figures from Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,400 Palestinians, injured over 175,000 others and damaged or destroyed around 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure during its war on Gaza.

articles.title: Saudi Vision 2030 offers new economic opportunities for Sri Lanka - Island.lk
articles.summary: Saudi Vision 2030 offers new economic opportunities for Sri Lanka  Island.lk
articles.full_text:
By Ifham Nizam
Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 is creating opportunities for Sri Lanka in trade, investment, renewable energy, tourism and employment while strengthening the longstanding friendship between the two countries.
Led by King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, the programme aims to diversify Saudi Arabia’s economy, attract international investment, develop new industries and reduce dependence on oil revenues.
Launched in 2016, Vision 2030 is built around three pillars: a vibrant society, a thriving economy and an ambitious nation. Its focus on tourism, technology, logistics, renewable energy, industrial development and private-sector growth aligns with Sri Lanka’s need for foreign investment, stronger exports, energy security and sustainable employment.
Trade and investment opportunities
The establishment of the first Saudi–Sri Lanka Joint Business Council in November 2025 created a platform for businesses to identify investment opportunities, develop partnerships and address trade barriers. Saudi participation in Sri Lanka Expo 2027 could further strengthen commercial ties.
Sri Lanka can expand exports of value-added tea, spices, apparel, rubber products and processed foods to Saudi Arabia. Better distribution networks, packaging and compliance with market standards would help local producers, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, compete more effectively.
Saudi investors could explore Sri Lankan tourism, logistics, food processing, renewable energy and export-oriented manufacturing. The goal should be long-term partnerships that create jobs, transfer technology and improve productivity rather than simply increasing trade.
Renewable energy and green investment
Energy is another promising area. Saudi Arabia’s diversification programme includes major investments in renewable energy and emerging technologies. Partnerships in solar power, battery storage, electricity infrastructure and energy efficiency could help Sri Lanka reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and improve energy security.
Cooperation could also include technical training and technology transfer. Saudi investment in sustainable tourism, modern agriculture, water management and infrastructure could create further opportunities if projects are commercially viable and supported by transparent regulations.
Vision 2030 seeks to make Saudi Arabia a major international tourism destination while improving services for pilgrims visiting Makkah and Madinah.
Sri Lanka could attract more Saudi visitors through better air connectivity, targeted marketing and partnerships with travel operators. Sri Lankan companies could also supply food, hospitality services and other products to Saudi Arabia’s expanding tourism sector.
Employment remains central to bilateral relations. Sri Lankan workers contribute to the Saudi economy, while their remittances provide valuable foreign exchange at home. As Saudi Arabia develops new industries, Sri Lanka can strengthen vocational training and skills-based recruitment in hospitality, healthcare, construction and technical services. Recognised qualifications, ethical recruitment and worker protection would benefit both countries.
Economic cooperation is complemented by Saudi Arabia’s distinctive spiritual role as custodian of Islam’s two holiest mosques.
Through the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques’ Guests Programme for Hajj, Umrah and Visit, King Salman approved the hosting, at his personal expense, of 1,000 male and female Umrah performers from around the world in June 2026. Implemented by the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs, Dawah and Guidance, the programme’s first group included 250 guests from 16 Asian countries, who visited Madinah and Makkah and took part in cultural and educational activities.
For those invited, performing Umrah and visiting the holy sites is a deeply meaningful religious experience. The initiative reflects Saudi Arabia’s commitment to facilitating worship and strengthening bonds among Muslim communities. It also complements Vision 2030’s Pilgrim Experience Programme, which aims to improve transport, accommodation, digital services and facilities for pilgrims.
This spiritual and cultural engagement adds a human dimension to commercial ties, helping deepen understanding between the two peoples.
Sri Lanka and Saudi Arabia established diplomatic relations in 1974, and their partnership has grown through trade, employment, development cooperation and diplomacy. The next step is to convert this goodwill into measurable results.
Sri Lanka needs a clear portfolio of viable projects, predictable regulations and efficient procedures to attract Saudi investment. Local businesses must be prepared to meet Saudi market requirements, while the Joint Business Council and Sri Lanka Expo 2027 can help connect investors and entrepreneurs.
The partnership should ultimately be judged by increased exports, productive investment, quality employment and the transfer of skills and technology.
Vision 2030 offers Sri Lanka an opportunity to build a more dynamic relationship with Saudi Arabia by combining commercial cooperation with diplomatic, spiritual and people-to-people ties. Together, the two countries can create lasting benefits for their economies and communities.

articles.title: Global oil prices hit highest level in 5 months amid attacks on ships, facilities - ABC7 New York
articles.summary: Global oil prices hit highest level in 5 months amid attacks on ships, facilities  ABC7 New York
articles.full_text:
Global oil prices have climbed more than 55% since the outbreak of the Iran war.
Global oil prices climbed to their highest level in five months on Tuesday after Iran and its Houthi allies claimed attacks on oil infrastructure in the Middle East.
The Brent crude futures price, a benchmark for global trading, topped $111 a barrel for the first time since May before retreating to $110.30 a barrel. The latest reading marks a rise of more than 55% since the Iran war began in late February.
An oil shortage continues to bedevil crude sellers, who typically pass along elevated costs to refiners, leading to higher prices at the pump.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, or UKMTO, on Tuesday issued an advisory after it received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces off the coast of Oman.
Separately, Iranian state-run media reported on Tuesday that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed that two oil tankers hit naval mines south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The reports came a day after Yemen-based Houthi militants claimed a wave of strikes on Saudia Arabia on Monday, including the Shaybah oil field as well as Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a port city near a key transport corridor on the Red Sea.
The West Texas Intermediate futures price, a benchmark index for U.S. trading, also jumped on Tuesday. The price of U.S. oil prices stands at $105.75, a rise of more than 60% since the outbreak of the war.
The jump in oil prices arrived as affordability marks a top concern for voters ahead of early November's midterm elections.
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. clocked in at $4.27 on Tuesday, according to AAA. That figure amounts to a rise of nearly $1.30 since the start late February.
The Middle East conflict drove up fuel prices and catapulted U.S. inflation to a three-year high in May, but inflation eased slightly over the summer after a preliminary peace agreement established an on-again, off-again pause in fighting.
The tentative accord between the U.S. and Iran expired in August, giving way to continued attacks on oil infrastructure and ships in the region.
The U.S. -- the world's largest oil producer -- imports a small amount of crude from the Middle East. Since oil and gas are sold on a global market, however, the shortage has sent prices rising for everyone, including U.S. drivers.
ABC News' Nasser Atta, Othon Leyva and Desiree Adib contributed to this report.

articles.title: A Jewish Currents Guide to the Israeli Elections - Jewish Currents
articles.summary: A Jewish Currents Guide to the Israeli Elections  Jewish CurrentsWhat Could Swing Israel’s Election? Thousands Living in the U.S.  The New York TimesWin or Lose, Netanyahu Has Reshaped Israeli Politics in His Image  Bloomberg.comIsraelis' Confidence in Elections Dips Ahead of Key Vote  Gallup NewsArab voter turnout could make or break Netanyahu in Israeli election  Reuters
articles.full_text:
The future of Israeli democracy. Top row, from left: Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett, and Mansour Abbas. Bottom row: Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot.
The Israeli general election is in a couple of days, and there’s not much to get excited about. The worst-case outcome is really, really bad; the best-case outcome isn’t very good. Here’s a conversation I’ve imagined between me and you about the vote, how to think about it, and what it exposes about the idea of a Jewish and democratic state.
Does this election even matter? The Netanyahu bloc and the opposition all agree on the most important issues: They won’t stop the occupation, and they won’t stop the genocide. So who cares who wins?
From where we sit here in the US, it looks a bit like there’s nothing at stake next week. The Zionist right and the Zionist center are aligned in their opposition to Palestinian liberation, and the Zionist center left often seems willing to go along with them. So what would change if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses? My initial thought, in fact, was to headline this article something like, “The Israeli Elections Don’t Matter,” and to be very cynical and flip about the whole thing. But then I talked to some people.
“Palestinians on the ground desperately need oxygen,” Amjad Iraqi, senior Israel/Palestine analyst at the International Crisis Group, told me. The end of Netanyahu’s 17 years of nearly-uninterrupted domination of Israeli politics wouldn’t end the occupation. But it would almost certainly unseat Itamar Ben-Gvir, the Kahanist who as national security minister wields control over Israel’s prisons and police, and Bezalel Smotrich, the fascist minister of finance, who also has enormous influence over the West Bank. “What I’m being told from the political prisoners’ view is you need to change Ben-Gvir,” Abed Abu Shehadeh, a political activist and community organizer in Jaffa, told me last week. And for Palestinians in the West Bank, he said, “it matters if Smotrich is involved.”
There’s no likely outcome of this election that’s going to feel good. But things can always get worse. “I listen very carefully to my Palestinian friends,” said Orly Noy, an editor at the Israeli news outlet Local Call, a member of the board of the human rights group B’Tselem, and a parliamentary candidate with the Joint List, a coalition of Palestinian parties. “Palestinian citizens inside Israel say, ‘We are next in line, and they will deport us forcefully.’”
The elections matter, then, if only to ease the extraordinarily dire situation into which the current government has pressed Palestinians. “Nobody’s talking about change,” Abu Shehadeh said. “Everybody’s talking about, how do we minimize damage, and how do we just survive this point in history?”
So what would minimize the damage?
A government that excludes Netanyahu and the Kahanists, and comes to some sort of an agreement with the Palestinian parties, might ease the situation. But it’s not a likely outcome. The Zionist opposition is fractious; what’s more, their anti-Arab racism, and the anti-Arab racism of their voters, makes an alliance with the Palestinian parties to keep Netanyahu out of power far from a sure thing.
Here’s everything you need to know about the elections next week.
Part I: The Pieces
Around a dozen parties and party alliances are likely to win seats in the Knesset. The key to grasping how they all fit together is to understand what the Zionist parties did to the Palestinian political leader Sami Abu Shehadeh, and what it tells us about democracy in the Jewish state.
Which electoral list is Sami Abu Shehadeh on?
None, anymore. Abu Shehadeh heads the leftist Balad party, one of the three Palestinian parties that banded together in this election to run as the Joint List, along with Ahmed Tibi’s Ta’al, and Hadash, a Palestinian-Jewish communist party.
Last month, the parties of the Zionist center and center left joined a hard-right effort to have Abu Shehadeh disqualified from running, over an article he wrote immediately after October 7th that called the Hamas attacks “an important historic event.” Their central claim was that he should be barred under a law that bans candidates who support “armed struggle” against the state; in a court filing, Abu Shehadeh denied supporting armed struggle. (“I am ready to sign off on every word in Abu Shehadeh’s article,” the Haaretz columnist Gideon Levy wrote last month. “Its only sin is the author’s national identity.”) The hard right has long sought to disqualify Palestinians and their parties from Knesset elections, but this was the first time it worked: Abu Shehadeh withdrew early this month to avoid setting a damaging legal precedent, after it became clear that the Supreme Court was poised to uphold the disqualification.
What was different this time?
Well, one thing that was different was that the entire Zionist political spectrum, from the hard right to the left, backed the disqualification campaign.
Why would they do that? Don’t these parties disagree with each other on policies and politics?
We’re in this moment in Israeli politics where you sometimes need to squint to tell the difference between the far right and the center.
On the hard right you’ve got Netanyahu’s nationalist Likud, the major conservative force in Israeli politics since its founding in the 1970s. You’ve also got important smaller parties: Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, a Kahanist party supported by settler extremists; and Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party, which represents the national-religious movement and which is running on a joint slate with Zehut, a far-right libertarian party led by Moshe Feiglin, who says he wants to “see Gaza empty [of Palestinians].” Another small far-right party, Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael, drew some attention earlier this fall as an upstart alternative to Smotrich’s party, though it’s now looking like it won’t win enough votes to earn a Knesset seat.
The far-right parties generally agree on a few basic things: Expanding and intensifying the settlement project, including through annexation; pushing Israel’s borders north into southern Lebanon, or at least maintaining an indefinite military presence there; and removing Palestinians from Gaza. Those generally aren’t the stated positions of the centrist parties. But Israel’s hard right has largely set the terms of the country’s political discourse for most of the last 50 years, and successive generations of Israelis have absorbed its dehumanizing rhetoric about Palestinians being inherently dangerous trespassers in need of violent domination. The centrist parties, run largely by the right’s castoffs and former allies, aren’t challenging this consensus. They’ve campaigned against the parties of the hard right while choosing not to meaningfully oppose them on their core positions of inflicting maximum punishment on the Palestinians.
The presumed leader of the centrists is Gadi Eisenkot. Israel’s former top general, who in 2006 formulated the Dahiya doctrine, an Israeli military strategy that calls for the use of overwhelming force against civilian infrastructure, Eisenkot was a non-voting member of the six-man Netanyahu-led war cabinet that directed the genocide in Gaza. He now leads Yashar, a rather nondescript centrist party. The other leading centrist is Naftali Bennett, who a decade ago led the predecessor to Smotrich’s far-right Religious Zionist Party. Bennett nominally shifted to the center after alienating the right in 2021 by bringing his party into a governing coalition that included the Palestinian party Ra’am; he’s now running at the head of B’Yachad, a new centrist alliance. There’s also Avigdor Lieberman of Yisrael Beiteinu, a far-right party that’s only grouped with the centrist opposition because of Lieberman’s abiding hatred for Netanyahu, and his refusal to sit with Netanyahu’s Haredi allies.
Instead of opposing Netanyahu on the Palestinian question, which really isn’t up for debate in mainstream Israeli politics, these parties—which would qualify as far-right in plenty of other countries—are focused on issues like his mishandling of Israel’s various ongoing wars, his responsibility for the October 7th attacks, the high cost of living in Israel, and the Haredi draft exemption, which has been a rising source of tension over the past two years.
Okay, so I suppose we shouldn’t be surprised that the centrist parties backed the disqualification. What about the center left?
They aren’t much better at this point. The center-left party in this race is The Democrats, formed in 2024 through a last-ditch merger between Labor, which once had a hegemonic grip on Israeli politics, and the small peacenik party Meretz. The liberal Zionist politics the party represents had effectively died out by the time of the last general elections in 2022, when Labor won just four seats and Meretz was wiped out, but the 2023 protests against Netanyahu’s proposed judicial overhaul did a bit to rejuvenate the movement. The combined party is led by Yair Golan, a former general whom the Israeli high command gently disciplined in 2007 after Associated Press cameras caught his troops using Palestinians as human shields. His party’s doing better in the polls than any liberal Zionist party has in years. But that seems to be an effect of the liberal Zionist bloc consolidating into a single party, and the personal popularity of Golan, rather than any surge in support for an end to the conflict.
Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats
What does Golan say about Israel’s oppression of Palestinians?
Golan is squishy on Palestinian statehood, eschews the language of seeking peace with the Palestinians, and doesn’t talk about the occupation. Early in the campaign, Noam Sheizaf, the journalist and activist who co-founded +972 Magazine, led a partly-successful effort to bring the anti-occupation left into The Democrats. articles.title: Toppling Iran’s regime is ‘primary objective,’ Netanyahu says after US talks - Iran International
articles.summary: Toppling Iran’s regime is ‘primary objective,’ Netanyahu says after US talks  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that toppling Iran’s regime was Israel’s “primary objective,” a day after discussing Iran with US War Secretary Pete Hegseth during an unannounced visit to Israel.
Netanyahu said he had also discussed bringing down Iran’s leadership with US President Donald Trump on Sunday, placing the issue at the center of his latest contacts with Washington.
“We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime — that is the primary objective,” Netanyahu said at the opening of the academic year at the new Tel Hai University in Kiryat Shmona, near the Lebanese border.
“I have spoken about this with President Trump more than once, including the day before yesterday.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday he is personally committed to “finishing the job” by toppling the Islamic Republic, which he described as the head of a “venomous octopus.”
Netanyahu said he had discussed the objective with US President Donald Trump… pic.twitter.com/8ZbbgFrF6w
— Iran International English (@IranIntl_En) October 20, 2026
His remarks did not indicate whether Trump had agreed to pursue that objective or committed to further military action.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran specialist and former head of the Iran branch in Israeli Defense Intelligence, told Iran International that while the two leaders might agree on military targets, their strategic objectives could diverge.
"Netanyahu seeks to topple the regime, and Trump seeks to reach a good agreement with the same regime that Netanyahu seeks to topple," he said.
Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials told Reuters. Netanyahu’s spokesman, Doron Spielman, confirmed that they met at Uvda air force base in Israel’s southern Negev desert.
Spielman said the talks covered regional threats and US-Israeli cooperation in confronting them through offensive and defensive measures.
Hegseth also thanked Israel for hosting US forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed Trump’s support for Netanyahu.
‘Finishing the job’
Speaking on Tuesday, Netanyahu linked his stated objective in Iran to Israel’s campaign against Hezbollah, saying the military had made major progress against the Lebanese group but pledging to “finish the job.”
“Finishing the job means bringing down the terrorist regime in Iran. It is the head of this poisonous octopus. You cut it off, and it will fall. We will also have peace with Lebanon,” he said.
Netanyahu argued that Iran’s leadership, even “battered, wounded and beaten,” would seek to pursue nuclear weapons and rebuild its regional network of allied armed groups.
“Therefore, the only way to prevent this is to bring down this regime, and then the elimination of Hezbollah will follow,” he said.
The Hegseth meeting came eight days before Israel’s October 27 election. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, ahead of the country’s first parliamentary vote since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
In his endorsement message, Trump praised Netanyahu’s role in confronting Iran and warned that Washington might have to act alone if another leader took office.
US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off a wider regional war. The latest consultations come amid renewed tensions between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz and intensifying attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi Arabia.
