articles.title: Iran’s Ghalibaf says US must meet seven conditions to rebuild trust - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Iran’s Ghalibaf says US must meet seven conditions to rebuild trust  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has said the United States must meet seven conditions to regain Iran’s trust, according to Mehr News Agency, as diplomatic efforts between Tehran and Washington remain deadlocked over the terms for ending the conflict and restoring maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The reported remarks underline Iran’s position that renewed negotiations require concrete steps from Washington rather than assurances alone. Ghalibaf, who has played a central role in Iran’s negotiating efforts, has previously linked the reopening of the strategic waterway to fulfilment of Tehran’s conditions under a June memorandum of understanding.
Iran links trust to concrete concessions
Ghalibaf said earlier this month that Iran would continue both military and diplomatic efforts and would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions were met. He also accused Washington of seeking to prolong negotiations and impose one-sided demands, according to reports of his October 4 remarks.
Iran’s demands have included an end to hostilities, the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, the release of frozen Iranian assets and relief from sanctions affecting its oil exports. Tehran has also sought guarantees concerning further military action and the treatment of Iranian commercial shipping. The full list of seven conditions has not been independently confirmed in a single official US-Iran document available publicly.
The dispute reflects a wider disagreement over the sequence of negotiations. Iran has prioritised ending hostilities and addressing maritime restrictions, while Washington has pressed for discussions that include Iran’s nuclear programme. The two sides have exchanged proposals through intermediaries, but no comprehensive agreement has been announced.
Strait of Hormuz remains a major point of tension
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important energy shipping routes, connecting the Persian Gulf with international markets. Disruptions to traffic through the waterway can affect oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, shipping costs and energy prices.
On October 18, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi reiterated Tehran’s proposal to restore normal passage through the strait within seven days if Washington accepted specified conditions, Reuters reported. The proposal has not resulted in a publicly announced agreement, and key disagreements remain unresolved.
The latest reported statement from Ghalibaf therefore signals continued pressure on Washington rather than confirmation of a diplomatic breakthrough. It also leaves open whether the conditions are negotiable individually or must be accepted as a package.
The next developments will depend on responses from US officials and any further proposals delivered through mediators. Neither side has publicly confirmed a final agreement or a date for a new round of direct negotiations.

articles.title: [不同来源] Russia, Iran Bilateral Relations: October 2026 Update - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: Russia, Iran Bilateral Relations: October 2026 Update  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
From holding meetings with the Gulf Cooperation Council members and bilateral meetings with the Foreign Ministers of Bahrain, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, the Russian Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov arrived in Tehran to hold discussions with Masoud Pezeshkian, the Iranian President, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
At the same time, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, held talks with Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref in Dushanbe, Tajikistan. Lavrov’s mission appears to have been diplomacy based, looking at ways to prevent further conflict in the Middle East and broker some agreements between Iran and especially Saudi Arabia, where Iran has attacked US air force bases. Mishustin’s meetings appear to have been more trade and investment related. We will deal with these separately as follows:
Lavrov’s Meetings With Pezeshkian
The discussions conveyed the views of GCC members – who Lavrov had met the day before and addressed the situation in the Gulf region and ways to resolve the international crisis. They also discussed further steps to strengthen coordination within the United Nations and expand cooperation through BRICS, the SCO, and the EAEU.
President Pezeshkian urged faster implementation of existing joint agreements, highlighting energy, transportation, trade, and power plant infrastructure. Lavrov stressed Russia and Iran’s alignment on global issues and the need for ongoing diplomatic talks. and noted that Moscow expects President Pezeshkian to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit scheduled in Moscow next week.
Discussions focused heavily on resolving the “acute international crisis” in the Middle East. Lavrov emphasized that Russia’s diplomatic efforts at the United Nations are aimed at preventing a larger-scale war, offering Moscow’s continued assistance to facilitate a peaceful resolution.
Much of these discussions would have been security related and not open for public disbursement.
Lavrov’s Meetings With Araghchi
This was the fourth meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers this year, in addition to 14 telephone conversations. The ministers reviewed the implementation of agreements reached during talks between President of Russia Vladimir Putin and President Pezeshkian on September 1, with particular attention paid to current issues in trade, economic and investment cooperation, as well as the implementation of major joint projects in the transport, logistics and energy sectors.
The ministers addressed ongoing insecurity in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi blamed U.S. and Israeli military aggression for the tensions, while Lavrov called for a return to conditions that secure freedom of navigation. Despite international pressure, Lavrov made it clear that Russia will not abandon its joint economic, energy, transport, and investment agreements with Tehran, and detailed that Russia is continuing to provide direct humanitarian aid to Iran, including shipments of essential medicines and food supplies.
Lavrov said that “Despite the challenging situation, which has repeatedly been mentioned, Russia has no intention to abandon the implementation of economic and investment agreements with Iran. Great prospects are opening up in hydrocarbon extraction and transportation. Russia’s contractor is continuing engineering surveys along the route of the future Rasht-Astara railway line project and will begin construction as soon as the Iranian side completes the processing of necessary documents.”
The meeting underscored a strengthening comprehensive strategic partnership rooted in a mutual defense and threat-countering pact signed in 2025. Araghchi remarked that “never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now”.
Lavrov’s Meetings With Rezaei
Lavrov also held talks with Major-General Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. Rezaei emphasized that Tehran is fully resolved to solidify and expand its long-term strategic and bilateral relations with Moscow, and noted that under the shifting regional circumstances, ongoing stability and security in the Middle East depend heavily on multilateral cooperation among regional countries, free from foreign coercion.
They reviewed joint economic initiatives, specifically highlighting the completion of strategic transport corridors as key drivers for regional stability and economic development, while Lavrov reaffirmed Russia’s robust support for Iran’s positions and initiatives across international forums, including the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Russia is heavily involved in developing Iran’s nuclear energy sector. Lavrov mentioned that Russian specialists are gradually returning to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, which was bombed by US aircraft earlier this year. Moscow and Tehran are looking to build eight new NPP in Iran in the coming years as the country seeks to modernise its energy supplies. The NPP technology being considered cannot be repurposed to manufacture nuclear weapons.
Mishustin’s Meetings With Aref
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, who has arrived in Tajikistan to attend a meeting of prime ministers from Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member countries, held talks with Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref also on October 19. The Russian delegation also included Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk, Minister of Economic Development Maxim Reshetnikov, Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko, Deputy Energy Minister Yevgeny Grabchak, and Deputy Finance Minister Alexey Sazanov.
They also discussed the construction of new reactors at the Bushehr NPP, as well as outstanding issues relating to the Racht-Astara railway, a key link in the western corridor of the INSTC. While Lavrov stated that Russia was still waiting for Iranian documentation procedures to be completed, Deputy Prime Minister Overchuk revealed that Iran has notified the Russian side about the completion of the buyout of land for the construction of the Rasht-Astara railway section. Overchuk said that “The negotiation participants exchanged opinions. In the first place, the status of implementation of our North-South project, the construction of the section of the future Rasht-Astara railway was discussed. The Iranian side assured us that the land plots have been bought. We expect documentary confirmation of the buyout. The creation of this railway line is already being carried out by the Russian contractor.”
Overchuk added that “Issues concerning construction in the Caspian Sea and transportation in the Caspian Sea, primarily food transportation, were also discussed.”
For his part, Mishustin said that “At the government level, we are prioritizing the expansion of trade and economic cooperation, our trade grew last year and continues increasing despite geopolitical challenges and sanctions” and added that the implementation of the free trade agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union and Iran is yielding positive results.
He said “We are also implementing major joint projects in the energy sector, including the peaceful use of nuclear energy, as well as in industry, transport infrastructure, and agriculture. The North-South Transport Corridor, which connects Eurasia to the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean, is being actively developed. This project of regional significance will provide direct access to the growing markets of the Asia-Pacific region and Africa and will facilitate the creation of new production and logistics chains across Eurasia.”
Bilateral trade between Russia and Iran reached about US$5.8 billion in 2025, marking an increase of more than 21% compared to the previous year. Lavrov mentioned that 2026 trade grew by over 10% during the first eight months of 2026.

In related news, Iran has completed a key railway line connecting its southern port of Chabahar with Zahedan near its border with Afghanistan, amid a US blockade of its ports and mounting economic pressure from the West. The 730-km rail link gives Tehran more flexibility to move cargo to neighboring countries from the port, which is being developed by India.
The railway is a key link in the INSTC, with Iran’s broader ambition is to connect its southern ports to transport networks connecting the Caspian Sea and beyond, operationalizing a vast land corridor for market access across Afghanistan, Central Asia, and Russia. It offers an overland trade route bypassing Pakistan to connect the Indian Ocean with Afghanistan, Central Asia, and Russia, and is funded by Iran’s National Development Fund after initial foreign participation stalled due to US sanctions.
The Chabahar route is 40% shorter and 30% less costly than the existing Suez Canal route for moving cargo. The line, which has 39 tunnels, 201 bridges, and 33 stations, is currently undergoing testing and expected to become operational early next year. It can also move about 7 million tons of cargo and 1 million passengers annually.
The route also allows India to bypass Pakistan to access Iranian markets, although sanctions and blockades remain a challenge. However, New Delhi and Tehran are actively engaged in smoothing out customs, logistics, and operational issues to maximize the line’s commercial potential. Former Indian Ambassador to Iran D.P. Srivastava has said ”Central Asia and Russia are closer to India if we take the land routes.”
It also links through to Afghanistan’s rail network to Kabul, which is poised to become a Central Asia transit hub. articles.title: Türkiye part of region with $872B infrastructure project pipeline: HSBC | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
articles.summary: Türkiye part of region with $872B infrastructure project pipeline: HSBC | Daily Sabah  Daily Sabah
articles.full_text:
Türkiye is part of a region that has an $872 billion pipeline of infrastructure projects, highlighting its investment potential and offering international and corporate investors greater exposure to the region ahead of 2030, according to a report from HSBC.
Investment in alternative logistics routes could mitigate the impact of the Iran war and make the Strait of Hormuz "redundant" in the next five years, HSBC Group CEO Georges Elhedery told an event in Dubai on Tuesday.
The report, published Monday and based on data from MEED, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform, covers the Middle East, North Africa and Türkiye (MENAT) region.
The $872 billion is part of a wider infrastructure pipeline worth $1.4 trillion.
The Iran war has shown how heavily the world relies on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf between Iran and Oman. A fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade previously passed through it.
The conflict is pushing Gulf nations to channel resources into energy pipelines to ports, Elhedery said. He said this investment will help the region weather the fallout.
"Of course, we do wish and hope to see a resolution to the conflict," he said, but "Hormuz, probably in five years' time, may become redundant."
"We do see this region being able to recover and then continue growing," he said. "It will mean a lot of investment."
A recent HSBC survey of over 1,600 business leaders and around 820 global institutional investors, meanwhile, found that they still considered the Gulf an attractive investment hub.
However, after growth of 3.3% in 2025, the World Bank last week forecast a deep economic contraction of 1.3% in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region this year due to the war. That should be followed by a strong but uneven rebound in 2027.
HSBC's report doesn't say which Turkish projects are included in the $872 billion or how much of it is in Türkiye.
The country's place in the grouping reflects its role as a route between the Gulf and Europe.
The most direct example is the Development Road, a planned corridor linking the Persian Gulf to Europe through Iraq and Türkiye. It complements the Middle Corridor, the route across Central Asia and the Caucasus.
Cargo leaving Iraq's Faw Port, on the Gulf coast in Iraq's far south, would travel about 1,200 kilometers by rail to Ovaköy, a crossing on the Türkiye-Iraq border in southeastern Türkiye.
Turkish officials have linked that project to Hormuz and said that, had the Development Road been completed, the world's energy supply would have been far less affected.
Earlier this month, Türkiye opened the Çerkezköy-Kapıkule section, the longest part of the Halkalı-Kapıkule high-speed rail line, extending the network to the EU border.
The line is 229 kilometers long. It begins on Istanbul's western edge and ends at Türkiye's main rail and road border crossing with Bulgaria, at Kapıkule near the northwestern city of Edirne.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said the line is a key component of the 2,094-kilometer Turkish section of the Development Road.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and United Arab Emirates Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Mumbai on Tuesday for trilateral discussions on regional energy security and shared economic priorities. The meeting brought together the three countries’ senior diplomats to explore cooperation in trade, investment, technology and other areas amid shifting regional and global economic conditions.
Rubio confirmed the meeting in a post on X, writing: “It was great to meet with Indian External Affairs Minister @DrSJaishankar and UAE Foreign Minister @ABZayed to discuss regional energy security and advance our shared economic priorities.” The UAE’s state news agency, WAM, separately confirmed the trilateral meeting took place in Mumbai on October 20.
Energy security at the centre of discussions
The meeting comes as energy supply, affordability and regional stability remain important concerns for major economies. India relies heavily on imported energy, making diversified supplies and stable international markets significant to its economic planning. The United States and the UAE are also important participants in global energy markets, giving the three countries shared interests in discussing supply security and economic resilience.
According to WAM, the officials explored opportunities to deepen cooperation in the economy, trade, investment, technology and artificial intelligence. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments and discussed efforts to strengthen security, stability and sustainable development. The agency did not announce a specific agreement or new policy commitment resulting from the meeting.
The talks also fit into broader efforts to strengthen India-US relations. Jaishankar said in a separate post on X that his bilateral meeting with Rubio covered trade, energy, technology, defence, people-to-people ties and regional developments. Rubio likewise said the bilateral discussion focused on energy security and defence cooperation, while reaffirming the importance of the US-India strategic partnership.
Economic ties and regional cooperation
For India, closer coordination with Washington and Abu Dhabi could support efforts to expand trade, attract investment and develop technology partnerships. The UAE and India already maintain a comprehensive strategic partnership and a comprehensive economic partnership agreement, while the United States and India have been pursuing broader cooperation across trade, defence and technology.
However, the trilateral meeting should not be interpreted as evidence that a new energy deal or joint initiative has been finalised. The public statements released after the discussions described areas of common interest but did not provide specific timelines, funding commitments or implementation measures.
Further diplomatic engagement will determine whether the discussions lead to concrete projects or additional agreements. Officials have yet to announce any formal follow-up mechanism or a date for another trilateral meeting.

articles.title: Can Strait of Hormuz become ‘redundant’ in 5 years as Iran war drags on? Here are the alternate routes for Gulf states - Livemint
articles.summary: Can Strait of Hormuz become ‘redundant’ in 5 years as Iran war drags on? Here are the alternate routes for Gulf states  Livemint
articles.full_text:
The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints, could become “redundant” within five years as Gulf nations invest in alternative pipelines, ports and logistics networks, HSBC Group CEO Georges Elhedery said on Tuesday, according to Reuters.
The Iran war has exposed the risks of relying on the narrow waterway for energy exports, prompting regional governments to explore routes that can transport crude oil to international markets without passing through the strait.
“We do see this region being able to recover and then continue growing. It will mean a lot of investment,” Elhedery said at the HSBC Future Forum in Dubai.
“Of course, we do wish and hope to see a resolution to the conflict ... But Hormuz, probably in five years' time, may become redundant,” he added, according to Reuters.
Alternatives to Hormuz are not entirely new. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) already operate crude oil pipelines that bypass the strait. The bigger question is whether expanding these routes and building new infrastructure can significantly reduce the Gulf's dependence on the waterway.
Diversifying supply routes could help reduce some of these risks.
Route: Abqaiq in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, is one of the most significant existing alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.
The pipeline transports crude oil from processing facilities in eastern Saudi Arabia across the Arabian Peninsula to Yanbu. From there, oil can be loaded onto tankers and shipped to international markets without passing through Hormuz.
The pipeline gives Saudi Arabia the option of redirecting substantial volumes of crude towards the Red Sea, reducing its reliance on shipping lanes inside the Persian Gulf.
Red Sea shipping also faces security risks due to the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Route: Habshan in Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.
The UAE has another major alternative in the Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline, also known as ADCOP.
The approximately 400-km pipeline connects onshore oil facilities at Habshan with Fujairah, which lies outside the Strait of Hormuz. The pipeline has a reported capacity of around 1.8 million barrels per day, as per reports.
The UAE already uses this route to export crude.
Fujairah allows the UAE to load crude onto tankers without sending them through Hormuz. Expanding pipeline capacity, storage facilities and port infrastructure could help the country maintain exports during future disruptions.
Beyond existing pipelines, Gulf countries could invest in additional pipeline capacity, export terminals, storage facilities and transport links connecting oil-producing regions with ports outside the strait.
The objective would be to build greater redundancy into regional energy supply chains.
New routes would also need to be commercially viable and capable of handling large volumes reliably.
The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), announced at the G20 Summit in New Delhi in September 2023, is another connectivity initiative attracting attention amid instability in the Middle East.
The proposed corridor aims to connect India with the Gulf and Europe through an integrated network of shipping routes, ports, railways and other infrastructure. Its broader objective is to improve trade and logistics connectivity between the three regions.
The ongoing crises in the Middle East, including the Gaza war, tensions involving Iran and the risk of disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, have strengthened the case for more resilient trade routes, according to Gérard Mestrallet, special envoy of the French president for IMEC.
“The difficulties — October 7, Gaza, Iran, Hormuz — have even increased the necessity to have a resilient corridor, offering several possibilities to the market,” Mestrallet said.
For India, IMEC's potential lies in strengthening connectivity with Gulf markets and Europe.
However, it is a proposed multimodal trade corridor, not an operational crude oil pipeline designed to carry the volumes currently shipped through the strait.
Existing pipeline alternatives offer a way to redirect some crude oil exports, but they cannot yet replicate the scale of flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
The IEA estimates that Saudi Arabia and the UAE have a combined 3.5 million to 5.5 million barrels per day of potential capacity on alternative routes that could bypass the strait. This compares with approximately 20 million barrels per day of oil shipments that passed through Hormuz in 2025.
The agency has also cautioned that the logistics required to reroute and export large volumes have not been robustly tested.
There is another important limitation: bypass pipelines primarily address crude oil exports. They do not automatically provide an alternative for all LNG shipments passing through Hormuz, including supplies from Qatar. Gas exports require specialised infrastructure.
Additional pipelines and export terminals could provide valuable flexibility during a crisis, but the scale of investment required to replicate its role remains substantial, making it unlikely that the Strait of Hormuz can be rendered entirely redundant in the near future.
With inputs from Reuters.

articles.title: Trump Endorsed Netanyahu. Israelis Must Prepare for What’s Next | Opinion - Newsweek
articles.summary: Trump Endorsed Netanyahu. Israelis Must Prepare for What’s Next | Opinion  Newsweek
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump has now done what Benjamin Netanyahu desperately needed: He has endorsed the Israeli prime minister a week before an election that could determine whether Israel remains a prosperous liberal democracy or continues its slide toward an elected autocracy.
Israeli voters should ignore him. And they should prepare for something potentially more consequential: Trump may not accept Netanyahu's removal even if the Israeli electorate votes for change.
The endorsement came Sunday, with Trump praising Netanyahu as a great wartime leader and partner against Iran. He even suggested that without Netanyahu, America might have to confront Iran alone. This is extraordinary language from an American president about the democratic choices of an allied country.
Trump remains popular in Israel, with considerable justification. His recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital, recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, Abraham Accords diplomacy and willingness to confront Iran earned him genuine gratitude. But supporting Israel and supporting Netanyahu are two very different things. Increasingly, they may be opposites.
The endorsement should surprise nobody. Trump has made a habit of interfering in other countries' elections on behalf of right-wing populists. In Poland last year, his administration dispatched Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to support nationalist presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki, who won. In Hungary this April, Vice President JD Vance traveled to Budapest to campaign for Viktor Orbán, who lost despite years spent consolidating control over the country's institutions.
Trump plainly admires strongmen, especially those who portray themselves as the authentic voice of the nation while treating political opponents, independent institutions and inconvenient legal constraints as obstacles to be overcome. Indeed, he aspires to the exact same style, with Trumpy embellishments like a gold-plated Oval Office.
Netanyahu belongs increasingly to this political family.
His coalition's assault on judicial independence, hostility toward the security establishment, attacks on independent institutions and efforts to concentrate power reflect a familiar populist project: preserving the appearance of democratic elections while weakening the checks that make democracy meaningful.
But the case against Netanyahu goes far beyond democratic norms. His record is a succession of national catastrophes, moral embarrassments and strategic errors, and another government dependent on the same coalition partners promises more.
Start with October 7, 2023, the worst security failure in Israel's history. Netanyahu presided over a system that catastrophically underestimated Hamas, leaving Israeli communities defenseless against mass murder and kidnapping. Three years later, he continues resisting the independent state commission of inquiry necessary to establish responsibility and prevent another disaster.
Then there are the wars. Netanyahu's supporters celebrate Israel's blows against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. Some were significant. But enormous military expenditure and sacrifice have not translated into a stable regional order, while the Gaza war has devastated Israel's international standing.
Worse, Netanyahu's political survival depends on parties whose demands threaten Israel from within.
The ultra-Orthodox parties insist on preserving sweeping military exemptions for Haredi men, even as other Israelis endure repeated and prolonged reserve mobilizations. Haredi boys attend schools without adequate mathematics, English or science instruction, while subsidies help sustain prolonged nonparticipation in the workforce.
With the Haredi population, now at a sixth of the country, growing rapidly, this is an economic and military time bomb. A shrinking proportion of Israelis cannot indefinitely finance the state, staff its military and sustain its technological economy. A brain drain that will impoverish Israel is a very real possibility—yet Netanyahu cannot enact meaningful reform without blowing up the coalition that keeps him in power.
His dependence on the far right is no less destructive. Ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have promoted an agenda of settlement expansion and confrontation in the West Bank, while extremist settler violence increasingly threatens Palestinian civilians, leading to multiple fatalities and further eroding Israel's standing. The government has done essentially nothing to confront this abomination. The past week’s attacks on an American photojournalist and European visitors illustrate the danger. The world is watching, and European economic sanctions beckon should Israel return the same coalition to power.
Israel depends on international investment, trade, financial relationships and technological cooperation. A sustained confrontation with Europe, followed by growing pressure in the United States, could mean a weaker currency, declining investment, higher borrowing costs and diminished prosperity.
Current polling strongly suggests that Netanyahu's existing bloc will fall short of a parliamentary majority. The parties seeking to replace him, together with the two Israeli-Arab parties, would command a majority of Knesset seats, although translating that arithmetic into a government would require difficult political compromises. That’s because Netanyahu, with his jackhammer racist propaganda, has made the opposition peevish about actually establishing a coalition that depends on Arabs.
That brings us to the danger beyond election day.
Suppose Netanyahu loses his majority, but the opposition struggles to assemble a coalition. Trump could decide that his endorsement was merely the opening move.
Imagine the American president telephoning Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett, two leading potential architects of an alternative government, and pressing them to join a Netanyahu-led coalition instead. Trump has demonstrated little respect for the convention that American presidents should not dictate the internal politics of democratic allies. Why assume he would stop at an endorsement?
He could argue that Israel needs unity against Iran, that Washington requires Netanyahu as its partner, or that American diplomatic support depends on a government Trump finds acceptable.
The greatest temptation would be Saudi Arabia.
Imagine Trump offering a historic normalization agreement with Riyadh if Eisenkot and Bennett agree to serve under Netanyahu. Such a promise could create enormous pressure, including from Israelis who understandably regard peace with Saudi Arabia as a strategic prize.
That’s where it gets interesting.
Such a gross intervention is largely unprecedented in the annals of serious democracies, yet there is something intriguing about it. I would not categorically exclude the possibility that Netanyahu, freed from dependence on his current extremist partners, might govern differently. There could even be an attempt to arrange a presidential pardon in his ongoing corruption trial, although a pre-conviction pardon would raise exceptional legal and constitutional questions.
That would amount to an extraordinary bargain: Netanyahu retains power, the opposition joins him, his legal troubles are somehow resolved, and Trump delivers Saudi normalization.
But there is a fundamental problem. Saudi Arabia is not Trump's property to distribute. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman would have to agree to an actual, credible arrangement, including whatever commitments Riyadh requires concerning Palestinian statehood and regional security. A vague American promise would be worthless. Only a concrete Saudi commitment, signed and enforceable, could make such a proposition remotely serious.
This is a low-probability scenario. But given Trump’s obsession with being seen—however preposterously—as a Nobel Prize-worthy peacemaker, I cannot rule it out. And if it turns out that Trump can drag Netanyahu in the direction of a workable accommodation with the Palestinians, organize peace with Saudi Arabia in the bargain, and (a very big if) it’s real (as opposed to a standard Trump boondoggle), it becomes fascinating. Netanyahu, with his infinite lust for power, boundless cynicism, and sharp instincts, would probably go along.
Of course, there is an opposite scenario as well—with the same Netanyahu-friendly potential outcome: that Trump and Netanyahu restart the Iran war and then invoke the emergency to try to neutralize the results of the Israeli election.
Either way, Eisenkot and Bennett would face a profound choice: whether a diplomatic breakthrough (or a new war) would justify perpetuating the leadership and political culture they have promised to replace. That could become one of the most fascinating choices in Israel's history.
For now, Israelis must distinguish gratitude toward Trump from obedience to him. Israel's election belongs to Israelis. And if they vote for change, their leaders must have the resolve to deliver it — not surrender the result to pressure from Washington.
Dan Perry is the former London-based Europe-Africa Editor and Cairo-based Middle East Editor of The Associated Press, chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and the author of two books.
The views expressed in this article are the writer’s own.

articles.full_text:
India on Tuesday expressed deep concern over the situation in West Asia and reaffirmed its support for efforts to restore peace and ensure the smooth flow of trade, as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met his UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Mumbai to review bilateral relations.
Sheikh Abdullah, who arrived in Mumbai on Monday, said the United Arab Emirates (UAE) was keen to further strengthen cooperation with India across various sectors, including trade, culture, education and people-to-people ties.
The UAE is currently India’s third-largest trading partner after China and the United States, with bilateral trade exceeding $100 billion.
At the beginning of the meeting, Jaishankar said the situation in the Gulf remained a matter of serious concern.
“The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern. We will continue to work together and support all efforts to promote dialogue and diplomacy,” he said.

Jaishankar said the India-UAE economic partnership continued to achieve new milestones despite global economic challenges and regional uncertainties.
Bilateral trade has crossed $100 billion since the two countries signed the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) in 2022.
He noted that mutual investments between the two countries had continued to grow, reflecting businesses’ confidence in each other’s economies.
Cooperation in defence, energy and technology is also taking on a strategic dimension, he added.
Sheikh Abdullah, who is also the UAE’s Deputy Prime Minister, said his country wanted to expand bilateral cooperation further amid the uncertainty caused by the conflict in West Asia.
He said the UAE considered it an honour to be one of India’s largest trading partners and that its leadership was committed to building a closer, stronger and more diversified relationship with New Delhi.
“We are very close but we want to be closer,” Sheikh Abdullah said.
He added that the UAE was keen to deepen cooperation with India in areas such as cultural exchanges, education and people-to-people connections.
Following the meeting, Jaishankar described his discussions with Sheikh Abdullah as productive in a social media post.
He said both sides had conducted a comprehensive review of their bilateral ties.
“The breadth and ambition of our cooperation is visible across the domains of trade, investments, energy, technology, logistics, defence, education and people-to-people ties,” Jaishankar said.
India and the UAE have held several high-level meetings and exchanges this year as both countries seek to strengthen their strategic partnership.
UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed visited India in January. In February, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khalid led the UAE delegation to the AI Impact Summit, while he also led the delegation at the BRICS Summit in September.

articles.title: Singapore, Qatar to elevate ties to Strategic Partnership; renew energy cooperation pact - AsiaOne.com
articles.summary: Singapore, Qatar to elevate ties to Strategic Partnership; renew energy cooperation pact  AsiaOne.com
articles.full_text:
Singapore and Qatar have agreed to work towards elevating bilateral ties to a Strategic Partnership, as leaders from both countries met in Doha on Monday (Oct 19) for the ninth Qatar-Singapore High-Level Joint Committee (HLJC).
If realised, the partnership will make Qatar Singapore's second Strategic Partner in the Middle East and marks a new milestone in relations between the two countries, according to a joint statement issued after the meeting.
The HLJC was co-chaired by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Qatar Emir Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al Thani, marking the first time in the platform's 20-year history that it was co-chaired by the leaders of both countries.
Both sides also reaffirmed their commitment to broadening cooperation in areas such as trade and investment, energy, sustainable development, security, education and human capital development.
The two leaders also welcomed the positive outcomes from the third meeting of the Implementation Monitoring Mechanism of the HLJC held earlier in September.
On artificial intelligence (AI), digitalisation, and emerging technologies, PM Wong and Emir Sheikh Tamim recognised that these areas have the potential to become an important bilateral cooperation pillar.
They also underscored the importance of trusted, secure and responsible digital and AI ecosystems, including cooperation on cybersecurity and digital resilience.
Separately, PM Wong and Emir Sheikh Tamim witnessed the exchange of the renewal of a memorandum of understanding between QatarEnergy and Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry on cooperation in liquefied natural gas (LNG) and low-carbon technology.
"This agreement will strengthen energy security between our countries," Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) said in a statement on Monday night.
In a joint statement after the HLJC meeting, the two countries said that the memorandum of understanding underscores their commitment to facilitating stable LNG procurement supply chains and energy security, especially in light of recent market developments.
Turning to developments in the Middle East, the leaders expressed serious concern over the situation in the region and underscored the importance of dialogue and diplomacy in promoting peace and stability.
They also stressed the importance of upholding navigational rights and freedoms in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and ensuring that international shipping routes remain open, safe and secure.
The two leaders also reaffirmed their shared commitment to a rules-based international order and multilateralism to collectively address global challenges.
Looking ahead, both sides said they look forward to Emir Sheikh Tamim's State Visit to Singapore, which will serve as an opportunity to launch the Qatar-Singapore Strategic Partnership.
"This will open up new opportunities for cooperation in areas such as trade and investment, energy security, AI and digitalisation," PM Wong wrote in a social media post after the HLJC.
Earlier during his three-day visit to Qatar, PM Wong met with his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Mohammed Bin Abdulrahman Bin Jassim Al Thani.
They discussed opportunities to deepen bilateral cooperation and exchanged views on developments in the Middle East. Prime Minister Wong also visited the National Museum of Qatar.
Earlier on Monday, PM Wong visited Qatar Foundation, where he met vice-chairperson Sheikha Hind Bint Hamad Al Thani and exchanged views on education, research and innovation.
The prime minister also attended a reception for overseas Singaporeans in the evening.
The next leg of his visit, beginning Oct 20, is to the United Arab Emirates.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs H E Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman bin Hassan bin Ali Al Thani speaking at the Global Security Forum yesterday
Doha, Qatar: Qatar will soon announce a new defence partnership with regional allies and a defence hub in the country, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs H E Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman bin Hassan bin Ali Al Thani said at the Global Security Forum.
Speaking in the opening session, “The Future of Alliances: Building Lasting Regional Security,” Deputy PM outlined Qatar’s assessment of regional security challenges, its defence priorities and the importance of strategic partnerships, while stressing that diplomacy and military preparedness must go hand in hand.
He said the planned initiatives form part of a defence strategy to build local capabilities in air defence, counter-drone measures, and cyber security and electronic warfare. “These were identified as priorities in a defence review conducted last year.”
The plan, he said, also covers ammunition, with Qatar either producing locally or investing in companies, alongside partners including the United States, the United Kingdom and France.
The Deputy Prime Minister said Qatar has faced three pronged threats since June 2025: violations of its sovereignty through external attacks, disruption of energy supplies from Qatar and the wider Gulf, and spillover from the conflict.
He warned that disrupted energy supplies would raise costs for consumers worldwide and said the shockwave had not yet reached the expected level.
He added that the instability in the Gulf would also disrupt east-west supply chains, Gulf aid to other nations, and Gulf investments abroad that create jobs in Europe and the United States. “These interconnected interests underscore the importance of maintaining security and stability across the Gulf,” he said.
The Deputy Prime Minister said Qatar is strengthening its own defence capabilities while continuing to work with allies and GCC partners to address emerging threats.
He described cooperation within the GCC as a foundation for regional security.
He also highlighted Qatar’s longstanding defence partnership with the United States, saying decades of cooperation had helped build military capabilities and improve the exchange of operational experience referring to air defence during the conflict.
Talking on Al Udeid Air Base, he emphasised that the facility is a Qatari base used by the United States and other international partners.
He said more than 20 countries had been represented there at certain times and that development of the facility would continue to meet the requirements of Qatar’s air force and army and its allies.
The Deputy PM said Qatar was also drawing lessons from attacks involving missiles, drones and other threats to ensure that its critical assets were better protected against future incidents. He stressed that Qatar would continue to strengthen its deterrence capabilities while remaining committed to preventing further escalation.
He said that mediation remained an essential part of Qatar’s strategy to prevent conflicts and support lasting regional stability. He described diplomacy and defence readiness as complementary, arguing that efforts to resolve disputes peacefully did not remove the need for a country to be prepared to protect itself.
Citing Qatar’s mediation between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, which he said began in 2022 and reached a conclusion in 2025, he noted that diplomatic initiatives often required sustained effort and patience.
On ongoing diplomatic efforts involving the United States and Iran, the Deputy PM said Qatar supported Pakistan’s mediation efforts and was working in coordination with partners, including Oman. He said the parties complemented one another through a collective approach, with the aim of reaching a resolution to the conflict.
On Iran, he said relations were built on trust until the events of June last year, with no incident before then. Lasting peace, he said, would require a regional dialogue involving the Gulf Cooperation Council states, Pakistan and Turkiye, in consultation with international allies.
“It should rest on trust and a non-aggression agreement that addresses concerns on all sides.” He pointed to Germany and France, which moved from decades of conflict to economic ties, beginning with Airbus, as an example.
He said that Qatar and the GCC oppose the imposition of transit fees in the Strait of Hormuz, except where provided for under applicable commercial law. He also warned that uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and other maritime routes would affect energy supplies, markets and consumers, expressing hope that an agreement to end the conflict could be reached soon.
Asked about attacks on Qatari interests, H E Sheikh Saoud said Qatar was surprised by the attack on the Ras Laffan gas facility, and by a later attack on a leased ship about five days after a memorandum was signed in Geneva.

Qatar and the Republic of Korea have reaffirmed their 52-year partnership, with Seoul expressing solidarity with Doha and highlighting cooperation in energy, infrastructure, culture and efforts to promote lasting regional peace.
Speaking at the Republic of Korea’s National Day reception in Doha on Monday, ambassador Jeepio Hong emphasised the importance of the two countries standing by each other during difficult times, while highlighting decades of co-operation spanning trade, investment, education and cultural exchange.
“It's a time for showcasing Korea, what Korea has to offer,” he told Gulf Times. “Our theme has always been about Qatar and Korea, about the friendship that we have.”
He said that Korean companies and citizens continue to play a key role in partnering with Qataris, adding that the embassy wanted to strengthen cultural understanding and share the Republic of Korea’s achievements with Qatar.
“Our desire is to spread the Korean culture, spread the friendship, and spread all the wonderful things that Korea has to offer for Qatar,” Hong said.
In his address, the envoy highlighted Korean workers' contribution to the Gulf’s development during the 1970s, when companies from the Republic of Korea began seeking opportunities in the region.
Their work helped transform infrastructure across the Gulf, while remittances supported the country’s own economic development.
“Part of modern Korea was built here, in these sands,” he said, describing the relationship as one in which both countries had benefited from each other’s ambitions and resources.
Energy co-operation remains a cornerstone of the partnership.
Qatar’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) has helped meet the Republic of Korea’s energy needs, while Korean shipbuilders have constructed some of the giant LNG carriers used to transport the fuel internationally.
Hong also highlighted co-operation in emerging sectors, including artificial intelligence (AI) and defence, alongside established links in healthcare, education and business.
Cultural and sporting ties have further strengthened relations.
Recalling the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, the envoy referred to the Republic of Korea’s dramatic qualification for the knockout stage and the joint performance by BTS singer Jungkook and Qatari singer Fahad al-Kubaisi at the tournament’s opening ceremony.
The reception also celebrated Korean culture through a demonstration by a team from Kukkiwon, the world headquarters of taekwondo.
The envoy welcomed Grand Master Shin Jae-geun, a pioneer of the martial art in Qatar who trained members of the country’s armed forces and coached its national team.
Addressing regional tensions, Hong expressed support for Qatar’s mediation efforts and its pursuit of lasting peace and safe passage through regional waters.
“The Republic of Korea stands in solidarity with Qatar,” he said, stressing that friendship must extend beyond ceremonial occasions.
Hong stressed that the relationship was grounded in a shared belief that a nation’s greatest wealth lies in its people, and that international partnerships are strongest when countries support one another through both prosperity and adversity.

articles.title: Rystad Energy: US-Iran deal would delay, not end, supply crisis - Hydrocarbon Engineering
articles.summary: Rystad Energy: US-Iran deal would delay, not end, supply crisis  Hydrocarbon Engineering
articles.full_text:
Even if a deal is struck, Rystad Energy cautions that the consequences for physical oil markets will be slower and more conditional than futures prices are currently pricing in.
Here is Rystad Energy’s market update from Chief Oil Analyst Paola Rodriguez-Masiu, based in Amsterdam, The Netherlands:
“A deal announcement would move futures further immediately, in fact even the potential of a deal is already triggering a decline in oil prices.
However, the physical market does not run on political timelines. Even under an optimistic scenario involving a 30-day phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, meaningful volume recovery would happen in June at the earliest, with processing port arrivals lagging by an additional four to six weeks after that.
Transit insurance markets need to reprice, vessel operators need verified and sustained access, and commercial confidence cannot be rebuilt overnight.
The six-to-eight-week lag between credible access conditions and real flow normalisation is not a conservative estimate, it is a structural feature of how shipping markets work. Global markets should not mistake a ceasefire headline for a supply headline.”
The possible peace framework as currently understood involves a moratorium on Iranian nuclear enrichment, sanctions relief, and a 30-day negotiating window, with a gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz phased over that same period.
This is not a resolution, it is a structured pause, a distinction that matters enormously for physical barrels. Rystad Energy’s prior estimate of six to eight weeks between a credible access condition and meaningful volume recovery remains intact.
Physical flows back to 80 - 90% of pre-disruption levels are a July story. Processing port arrivals lag by an additional four to six weeks.
The price impact of a deal is being felt immediately in futures. The physical market will take considerably longer to agree.
Several signals distinguish today’s situation from prior episodes where US proposals have been floated and failed to materialise.
China has changed its posture. Iran’s Foreign Minister Araghchi made his first visit to Beijing since the war began on February 28.
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi publicly called for a comprehensive ceasefire and for Hormuz to reopen “as soon as possible.”
Beijing describing itself as “deeply distressed” while hosting Iran’s top diplomat is a materially different posture than anything seen to date.
China’s leverage over Iranian oil revenues gives it tools Washington does not have, and there is now direct evidence it is deploying them.
The US has made a tangible operational concession. President Trump has paused US efforts to escort commercial vessels through the Strait, explicitly to give a deal room to close.
That is a significant shift in operational posture.
The IRGC is silent. Unlike every previous juncture where US proposals have been floated, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has not commented.
Navigation statements aside, there has been no significant political response or official positioning. In Rystad Energy’s view, that silence is analytically significant.

articles.title: Alberta snubs separatists as majority votes to remain part of Canada
articles.summary: Albertans voted to remain in Canada in the province's first referendum on separation, a key victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney amid a trade war with the U.S. and national unity...
articles.full_text:
Albertans voted to remain in Canada in the province's first referendum on separation, a key victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney amid a trade war with the U.S. and national unity challenges.
With 75% of votes counted as of 5:45 a.m. Tuesday, 76% of Albertans voted to remain in Canada. Only 24% supported separation, though the referendum was nonbinding.
"Albertans made a clear choice," Carney said in a statement. "They chose unity, to build together and care for each other."
"Canada is greater than the sum of its parts," he said.
Pollsters and analysts dismissed the possibility of a separatist victory in Monday's vote, citing data showing only about one-third of residents in the energy-rich western province supported a future referendum on separation.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who announced the referendum in May, said in a statement she was "very pleased" that early results showed widespread support for remaining.
Smith said she would address Albertans at 6:45 p.m. Tuesday to discuss "where our province goes from here."
A small but vocal group of separatists campaigned for months for an independent Alberta, arguing the province's energy wealth subsidized poorer Canadian provinces and that it would be far richer free of Ottawa's bureaucracy.
Last week, Carney told a rally in Calgary that voting to leave Canada would be "a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division."
There was no immediate reaction to the vote's outcome from President Donald Trump, who repeatedly talked about the U.S. annexing Canada. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, discussing Alberta in January, said, "I think we should let them come down into the U.S."
Monday's vote was the second time in two weeks that Carney faced a separatist challenge. An independence-minded party won power in French-speaking Quebec on Oct. 5 but fell short of the majority needed to fulfill a vow to hold a vote on separation.
Quebec held referendums on independence in 1980 and 1995, but both failed.
Carney, who grew up mostly in Alberta, acknowledges Albertans often feel slighted by Ottawa. He noted his government fast-tracked a proposed new pipeline with Alberta and the federal government as majority owners. He also pointed to Alberta's critical role in helping Canada reduce its dependence on the U.S.
First Nations groups also objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province's creation within Canada.
The result is unlikely to end the independence movement. Before the referendum, some separatist leaders said they would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans wanted to remain.
According to data released Oct. 16 by pollster Angus Reid, 62% of Albertans believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement."
The vote Monday also included nine other nonbinding questions on proposed measures to strengthen the province's hand when dealing with Ottawa.
These covered immigration, access to provincial services – such as education, social care and health care – and voter identification requirements.
Provisional results showed voters backed eight of the nine measures, but some with only slim majorities.

"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them. But of course, if there are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations. It's absolutely clear," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo.
Zelenskyy also said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian missile attacks that he said occurred without enough notice.
For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country's military has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. He said such intelligence saves lives by allowing alerts to the public and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.
Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day.
"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."
In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help during meetings in Norway.
Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Jared Kushner, another envoy who is U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was due to attend a meeting with Zelenskyy by videoconference.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with Zelenskyy in Norway's capital.
"We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace," Zelenskyy said in a post on X after he arrived in Oslo. He said officials gathered in Norway would discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and joint production of weapons.
Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Moscow hopes a meeting in Russia between the envoys and Russian President Vladimir Putin can be organized soon, perhaps as early as Wednesday.
"We highly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators," Peskov said.
With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and Trump sour again, the Ukrainian leader said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia.
That conversation came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also said he sought Rubio's help to ensure that the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv received no or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days.
The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.
Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.
"Nothing has changed," he told reporters.
The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.
With the Russian army held up on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while robbing it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say.
European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.
European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for ... one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.
Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.

articles.title: Russia builds long-range radar in Kaliningrad: Reports
articles.summary: Russia has constructed a powerful radar facility in its Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad capable of tracking aircraft, missiles and ships as far as 3,200 kilometers (2,000 miles)...
articles.full_text:
Russia has constructed a powerful radar facility in its Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad capable of tracking aircraft, missiles and ships as far as 3,200 kilometers (2,000 miles) away, British media reported.
The system could expand Moscow’s surveillance capabilities in northern and western Europe, including the U.K., The Times newspaper reported Monday, citing satellite imagery.
Located near the town of Gvardeysk, the installation is in Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory bordering NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
The facility features three radiating arms of antenna masts, each 500 meters (1,640 feet) long, according to the report.
The configuration suggests the installation could be an over-the-horizon (OTH) radar – technology designed to detect targets beyond the line of sight of conventional radar systems.
OTH radars use high-frequency radio waves that can reflect off the ionosphere, allowing them to detect potential targets over much greater distances than conventional systems.
The radar’s reported range is estimated at between 885 and 3,200 kilometers (550 to 2,000 miles), potentially enabling Russia to monitor military activity across large parts of Europe.
Kaliningrad is strategically important to Moscow because of its position on the Baltic Sea, between Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members.

articles.title: Romania's parliament approves new PM, ends political deadlock
articles.summary: Romania's parliament confirmed independent Luca Niculescu as prime minister Tuesday, breaking nearly six months of political gridlock that had shaken investor confidence and raised...
articles.full_text:
Romania's parliament confirmed independent Luca Niculescu as prime minister Tuesday, breaking nearly six months of political gridlock that had shaken investor confidence and raised concerns over the country's investment-grade credit rating.
Niculescu, 55, won a parliamentary vote of confidence after putting together a minority government of leftists and technocrats following his nomination by centrist President Nicusor Dan.
It was Dan's fourth attempt to install a government in the NATO and European Union member state since a pro-European broad coalition cabinet collapsed in early May.
Niculescu, who has served as a diplomat and deputy foreign minister and was formerly a journalist, secured 280 votes in parliament, easily passing the 233 required.
But he has a daunting task in trying to tackle Romania's economic problems, and political analysts said his government could be short-lived.
He must try to make further cuts to one of the EU's largest budget deficits while propping up a contracting economy, eliminating an additional turnover tax on companies and raising pensions that fiscal constraints kept frozen for two years.
"I am not asking for a blank check," Niculescu told lawmakers before the vote. "I am asking you to understand Romania needs a government with full powers after so many months of crisis."
If Niculescu's government cannot get a deficit-reducing budget plan for 2027 through parliament in December, it will risk a ratings downgrade after it already sits on the last rung of investment grade, all the major ratings agencies have said.
Romania has agreed with Brussels to bring its budget deficit below 3% of economic output - from over 9% in 2024 and an expected 6.2% this year - by 2030. On Monday, Moody's said the green light for Niculescu's cabinet would allow for the timely adoption of a 2027 budget that supports fiscal correction.
The leftist Social Democrats (PSD), which joined Niculescu's government after toppling their former four-party coalition in early May, said they would re-assess their support in six months.
Niculescu has also signed political pacts with two centre-right parties from the former coalition in which they agree not to file any no-confidence votes before March 2027.
The Eurasia Group think tank said a new government "would restore short-term stability and unblock policymaking."
"Ultimately, Niculescu's ability to balance competing demands and maintain parliamentary support will determine whether the government can sustain stability beyond April 2027," it said.
Romania's next parliamentary election is due by late 2028. The country has never held an early election.
The opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians, which has been critical of Brussels, defence procurement and aid for Ukraine, leads opinion polls with about 40% support.
(Reporting by Luiza Ilie, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

articles.title: Sudan army strike kills 53 in disputed territory with S. Sudan
articles.summary: A Sudanese army drone strike killed 53 people at a market in a region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, local authorities said Tuesday, marking the latest in a series of deadly at...
articles.full_text:
A Sudanese army drone strike killed 53 people at a market in a region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, local authorities said Tuesday, marking the latest in a series of deadly attacks.
Authorities in Abyei district said the strike hit Amiet market Monday. They accused the army of launching 22 munitions in the attack, which also wounded at least 27 people.
"The casualties comprise vulnerable civilian populations, including women, children, the elderly, local merchants, members of the host Ngok Dinka community, South Sudanese returnees and Sudanese refugees who had sought sanctuary from the broader regional conflict," the authorities said.
From Sunday to Monday, strikes across Sudan killed more than 100 people. The country is engaged in a brutal war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that began in April 2023.
Both Sudan and South Sudan claim Abyei district. South Sudan split from its northern neighbor in 2011 following decades of conflict.
The Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) controls parts of the district. It is a splinter from the organization that fought for South Sudan's independence. The group is split in two, and each faction supports opposite sides in Sudan's war.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry said it summoned the Sudanese ambassador over the attack, condemning it "in the strongest terms possible."
The ministry accused the Sudanese army of striking multiple locations within the market, used as a transit point for goods to areas controlled by the RSF.
Sudan's war, which multiple outside powers have fueled, has triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and killed hundreds of thousands of people.
The deadliest strike during the recent wave came near a market Sunday evening in al-Dibab town in the southwestern state of West Kordofan, controlled by the RSF.
Residents and medical workers said a drone struck a transport hub where villagers gathered after a market day to find rides home, killing 80 people.
Ahmed Abakar Wadi, a resident who helped bury victims, told AFP at least 50 bodies were recovered at the scene, including that of his brother.
Another 47 wounded people were taken to the nearby town of al-Mujlad where 30 later died of their injuries, according to a medical source.
"The drone struck once, and then came back 10 minutes later and struck again," Wadi told AFP.
The RSF's self-declared Tasis administration and the Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out Sunday's attack.
The military has not commented.
It was one of the deadliest attacks in Kordofan, an oil-rich region linking western and eastern Sudan where the army and the RSF have been battling for territory.
Strikes also hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala in South Darfur and the army-controlled capital Khartoum.
More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: Social unrest sweeping through France to Albania sets Europe ablaze
articles.summary: A housing crisis, rising fuel costs and deteriorating public services have sparked a wave of autumn protests across Europe where weeks of demonstrations in France, Italy and Albani...
articles.full_text:
A housing crisis, rising fuel costs and deteriorating public services have sparked a wave of autumn protests across Europe where weeks of demonstrations in France, Italy and Albania have seen arrests and violence, while tent camps have formed in Spain and Portugal to protest unaffordable housing.
Young Europeans are experiencing "a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control," said Maria Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. "And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets."
Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent arson attacks, cyberattacks and other acts of sabotage in NATO countries.
Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction, writing Monday on his Truth Social platform: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Many of the protests have been fueled by frustrated young people. Other actors, including black-clad, masked agitators, have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants.
In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they describe as understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighborhoods.
The protests broadened as France's CGT labor union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services.
Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend’s unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.
In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds have been injured.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday’s violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police.
"Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address.
In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year.
In Madrid's central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities.
The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, leading Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call for an early election in November. A general strike also was called for November – the first in 14 years.
Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain's overtourism and housing challenges.
Spain's minimum wage is 1,221 euros ($1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around 1,130 euros (about $1,270), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansion.
"Most of my paycheck goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do," said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. "This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city."
"Italia in Piazza," or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, health care, education and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2% in September, surpassing the eurozone’s 3.8%, according to government data.
The peaceful marches were followed by violent riots in Turin and Bologna and in Italy's finance and fashion capital of Milan, where masked rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Milan police said 271 people were arrested - most of them minors - and 14 security officers were injured during two days of unrest.
Now a newly formed group calling itself the "Oct. 17 Movement" has announced what it describes as a "permanent mobilization" to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy.
Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania's capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government "Flamingo" movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Rama has condemned the protesters as "ideologized and radicalized" by antifa , an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants. President Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization in the United States.
Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.
In Serbia, the university students leading mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are challenging an attempted return to power by the Balkan country’s former populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections.
The former authoritarian president is aiming to be named prime minister after the Oct. 25 vote. The youth-backed Students’ List party is believed to be running close to Vucic’s party, making the outcome uncertain and fueling fears of possible violence.
